What Kind of Book Is This? The Same “Three Times,” Two Ways to Read It
Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path. (Psalm 119:105)

Brothers and sisters, peace to you! I’d like you to imagine two slips of paper. The first is a pharmacy bag, and on it is written: three times a day, after meals. The second is a love letter, and on it is written: I think of you three times a day.

If you read the love letter the way you read the pharmacy bag, you might write back and ask: excuse me, which three time slots? Before meals or after? That relationship has probably come to an end. Turn it around, read the pharmacy bag with the romance of a love letter, decide that “three times is simply an expression of feeling,” and you’ll be checking into the hospital.

Honestly, a good deal of the confusion people have about the Bible today comes from right here. Some treat poetry like a geological report, some treat genealogies like a blessing, and some treat Revelation like next year’s calendar. As we step into the first gallery of the Bible Hall, let’s hold off on asking “can this book be trusted?” and ask a more basic question first: what kind of book is this, really?
1. It Turns Out to Be a Library
Even the house numbers were nailed on later

Let me tell you something that might surprise you. When the apostle John wrote his Gospel, he had no idea he was writing “John 3:16.” The chapter divisions we use today go back to the early thirteenth century and Stephen Langton, Archbishop of Canterbury. The New Testament’s verses had to wait until 1551, when a printer named Estienne numbered them.

So friends, if you’ve ever felt that the verse breaks are a little strange, with one sentence cut in two, you weren’t imagining it. These house numbers are very convenient, and we depend on them today to find any passage, but the original authors never nailed them up. Next time you read the Bible, forget the numbers now and then and read straight on. You’ll discover that these books are really one whole letter, one whole story.

The English word “Bible” comes from the Greek ta biblia, literally the plural “books.” The Protestant Bible has sixty-six books, thirty-nine in the Old Testament and twenty-seven in the New. The Catholic and Orthodox Old Testaments have more, and that is the topic of the next gallery.

There are three languages. The Old Testament is mainly Hebrew, but some passages of Ezra and Daniel are in Aramaic, and so is one verse in Jeremiah chapter ten. The New Testament is in the Greek commonly used around the Mediterranean at the time. God did not open a course in some “official language of heaven” and tell everyone to enroll. He spoke to people in the words ordinary folks used in the marketplace.

Church people often say the Bible has about forty authors and was written over about fifteen hundred years. That figure can be used, but we have to be clear: it’s an estimate, and it assumes the traditional authors and dates of most of the books. Many scholars would give a different answer. We don’t know the authors of many psalms, and no one knows to this day who wrote Hebrews. I would rather state the conditions plainly than have a friend feel deceived later on.
Spiritual meaning: God is willing to stoop

Think about it. Almighty God could simply have dropped an instruction manual from heaven, cover stamped in gold, no translation needed. He did not. He used a shepherd’s poems, an exile’s tears, a fisherman’s letters, a tax collector’s records.
God, having in the past spoken to the fathers through the prophets at many times and in various ways, has at the end of these days spoken to us by his Son, (Hebrews 1:1-2)
“At many times and in various ways.” What beautiful words those are. A God willing to speak to people like this is a God willing to bend down.
Every shelf has its own way of being read

When you walk into a library, you don’t read a cookbook, a legal statute and a collection of poems in the same frame of mind. The Bible is the same. Narrative books tell you what happened, but recording something does not mean approving of it. David sinned, and the Bible writes it down as it was; no one concludes from this that the Bible encourages adultery. The books of the law are the terms of God’s covenant with ancient Israel, and you have to ask how they are fulfilled in Christ. The Psalms speak in images. “Yahweh is my rock,” and you don’t need to find out whether it’s granite or limestone.

Proverbs is the easiest to misread. Proverbs mostly gives general patterns, not guarantees. Some parents raise their child very well and the child still goes astray, and the last thing they need is someone holding up Proverbs to accuse them. The Bible itself reminds us of this. In Proverbs 26:4-5, two verses in a row, one says “Don’t answer a fool according to his folly,” and the next says “Answer a fool according to his folly.” The editor wasn’t asleep. He put them together on purpose, as if to say: wisdom is knowing which verse today calls for.

Apocalyptic literature calls for even more care. In every generation people have held Revelation up against the newspaper and worked out the date of the Lord’s return, and so far every one of them has been wrong. We long for the Lord’s return, and we don’t go calculating the day.

Letters have their own way of being read, too. Reading a letter is like overhearing one half of a phone call at the next table in a restaurant: you hear Paul’s answer without hearing the Corinthians’ question. So before reading, first ask: who is this letter written to? What has been happening to them? The Gospels are another kind of book again. The four authors each made their own selections, and their writing is close to ancient biography. It is no day-by-day dashcam recording.

But let me also tap the brakes. Talking about genre doesn’t hand us a remote control, so that whenever we see a verse we don’t like we can press a button and say, “That’s a metaphor.” Genre exists to help us hear what the author wants to say; it is not there to make the author be quiet. Ancient Israel was a largely oral society, and scholars like Walton and Sandy remind us not to force today’s picture of publishing onto it, or we will ask the wrong questions without even knowing it.
Spiritual meaning: understanding is part of love

When you truly love someone, you want to understand what they are saying, and not merely grab one sentence and put it to use. In Nehemiah’s day, when Ezra led the people in reading Scripture, the Bible records it like this:
They read in the book, in the law of God, distinctly; and they gave the sense, so that they understood the reading. (Nehemiah 8:8)
More than two thousand years ago, reading Scripture already included this step of giving the sense. To read the Bible rightly is to take seriously the God who speaks.
3. The Whole Library Points to One Person
The main character of the book

Now we come to the most important point. On Easter day two disciples were walking on the road to Emmaus, and their hopes had been shattered. A stranger came and walked with them. It was the risen Jesus, but they did not recognize Him.
Beginning from Moses and from all the prophets, he explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself. (Luke 24:27)

How I would love to have heard that class! Jesus walked about eleven kilometers along that road and took them through the whole library. We don’t know the details of how He taught it, but we do know how He read it: these books, in the end, all point to Him.
Yet to the religious leaders who knew the Scriptures best at that time, Jesus said something very heavy:
“You search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life; and these are they which testify about me. (John 5:39)
Brothers and sisters, a person can know the verses by heart and still miss the book’s main character standing right in front of him. That can happen, and it has happened.

Two scholars, Bartholomew and Goheen, compare the Bible’s story to a drama in six acts. Act one, creation. Act two, the fall. Act three, God chooses Israel. Act four, Jesus Christ comes. Act five, the church is sent. Act six, all things are made new. Friends, what makes this picture so useful is that you and I are not an audience sitting in the seats. We are living in act five. The ending of the script has already been written and the main character has already won, but this act is still being performed, and your lines today must be spoken by you, at home, at the office, in front of your children.

So when you read a passage, you can ask two questions: which act is this in? And how does it relate to the main character of act four? Those two questions alone can bring to life many Old Testament passages people can’t get through. The sacrifices in Leviticus, for example, are hard going on their own. Set them in this drama and you will understand why John the Baptist pointed to Jesus and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God.”
Giving the other side a fair hearing

A skeptical friend might ask: Pastor, with so many authors and one main storyline, could that have been created by later editors and by the church as they selected and ordered the books? That’s a good question. My answer is: yes, there is a human element. The arrangement of the canon is itself a kind of reading, so “consistency” alone cannot prove the Bible comes from God, and I won’t tell you that it does.

What I can say is that this thread deserves an explanation. The Christian explanation is that the one God revealed Himself in history step by step, and finally, at the cross and the empty tomb, gathered all the threads together. Whether to accept that explanation is up to you. You’re welcome to read it and see for yourself.
Spiritual meaning: read until you reach Christ

By early 2026, seven hundred ninety-five languages around the world had a complete Bible and four thousand one hundred twenty-one had at least a part of it. Those are the figures of United Bible Societies. Another number is just as true, though: more than three thousand two hundred languages still don’t have a single verse. The Chinese Union Version was the fruit of missionaries’ work from 1890 to 1919. The book in our hands was delivered to us by people who gave their lives to it. Don’t let it just sit on the shelf as decoration.

Take three things home today. First, the Bible is a library, and each shelf has its own way of being read. Second, we honestly face the debates about authors and dates, and we don’t present estimates as iron laws. Third, the whole library finally points to Jesus.

In 321 language: the Bible is my standard, and a standard must be understood before it can be used. Jesus is my example, and this is how He Himself read Scripture. Change your mindset, and your life will change, and then your daily living will change. If you have always treated the Bible as a reference book for looking up answers, change that mindset today: it is what a living God has said to you, at many times and in various ways. This week choose a short book you’ve never read and read it in one sitting. Ruth or Philippians would both do.

Let us pray together. Lord, you have spoken to people at many times and in various ways, and finally you have shown yourself to us through your Son. Forgive us for so often treating your word as a tool, using it to back up what we have already decided. May the Holy Spirit open our hearts, so that we read your word rightly and meet, in its words, the Christ who laid down His life for us and rose again. In Jesus’ name, amen.
1. Have you ever been confused because you misread the genre, such as treating Proverbs as a guarantee or taking poetry as a literal description? How did you come to understand it later?
2. When it comes to claims like “about forty authors over about fifteen hundred years,” how do you think we should put it to friends who don’t yet believe, so as to be honest?
3. Which short book will you read in one sitting this week? When you’ve finished, come back and share how that book points to Christ.
The Dead Sea Scrolls: A Thousand-Year-Old Notebook
The grass withers, the flower fades; but the word of our God stands forever. (Isaiah 40:8)

Brothers and sisters, peace to you! Imagine your family has a recipe for braised pork, handed down for more than ten generations. Grandma says it’s the family recipe and not one thing about it has changed. You can’t help wondering: after all that time, has the flavor really not drifted? Then one day, while renovating the old house, you dig a thousand-year-old notebook out of the wall. You open it, and your first reaction is relief: the main ingredients and proportions are roughly the same. Then you start to laugh. This page has an extra pinch of star anise, that page is in a different hand, and some distant nephew’s version leaves one ingredient out.

Today’s gallery is the Bible’s old notebook. Between late 1946 and early 1947, a few shepherds found some clay jars in a cave by the Dead Sea, and inside them were parchment scrolls. They came to be called one of the most important archaeological discoveries of the twentieth century. But today I don’t only want to tell you how exciting they are. I also want you to see that extra pinch of star anise. A faith that is afraid of being checked isn’t worth entrusting your life to.
1. Checking the math on a thousand years

By 1956, eleven scroll caves had been found in all. Counting methods differ, but people generally speak of a little over nine hundred to nine hundred eighty-some manuscripts, most of them broken into fragments. About two hundred thirty-five are biblical books, dating from the third century BC to the first century AD, and every book of the Hebrew Bible except Esther has at least a fragment.

Before this, the most complete Hebrew Bible manuscripts we had in hand came from around the tenth century AD. The Dead Sea Scrolls suddenly pushed the evidence back a thousand years. Think about it, friends. It’s as if a teacher gave you a math problem, you worked on it for a thousand years, and today you suddenly got hold of the original scratch paper, so you could check it step by step.

The most famous one is the Great Isaiah Scroll, more than seven meters long, with fifty-four columns. All sixty-six chapters are there, in the same order we have today. The handwriting dates to about 125 to 100 BC, and the carbon-dating range is somewhat wider. In other words, this scroll was already there more than a century before Jesus was born.

People online often say this scroll is ninety-five percent word-for-word identical to today’s Bible. Please hold off on forwarding that. The truth is that, compared with the Masoretic Text, it has more than twenty-six hundred variants. Most are small differences of spelling, single words and word order, like “color” and “colour,” or the two ways of writing the first character of Taiwan’s name in Chinese. But a few affect a whole verse. Another Isaiah scroll, 1QIsab, is much closer to the Masoretic Text. So we can say the whole is highly consistent, and we must also say the differences are real.
Spiritual meaning: treasure in clay vessels

There is one detail I especially love. In that passage of Isaiah 40, “The grass withers, the flower fades,” part of the text in the Great Scroll was added later by another hand. Scholars debate how to explain this passage, and some think it is the longer form from another textual tradition.

Look at that. Right beside the famous line “the word of our God stands forever,” we can see a scribe’s hand. God’s word has never stood forever because scribes’ hands never trembled. God is glad to put His treasure in clay jars, so that everyone will know the power comes from Him.
But we have this treasure in clay vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God and not from ourselves. (2 Corinthians 4:7)
2. That extra pinch of star anise

Sunday school friends, please take note: this next question may affect your teaching materials. The Chinese Union Version says Goliath’s height was “six cubits and a span,” and the World English Bible we read today says the same. That works out to about 2.9 meters. But the Dead Sea Scroll of Samuel, 4QSama, the Greek Septuagint, and the historian Josephus all say four cubits and a span, about two meters.
A champion out of the camp of the Philistines named Goliath of Gath, whose height was six cubits and a span went out. (1 Samuel 17:4)

A two-meter giant was still terrifying in the ancient world, especially since people then were generally shorter than we are today. David’s courage isn’t discounted one bit. Many scholars think the larger number grew in transmission, and some scholars hold a different view. Our faith loses nothing by this, though the Sunday school picture may need a little adjusting.
One passage more, one book shorter, one verse missing

Let’s look at other examples. That same 4QSama has an extra passage at the end of 1 Samuel 10, explaining how Nahash, king of the Ammonites, gouged out people’s right eyes, and some modern English translations have adopted it. Jeremiah comes in two versions: the Septuagint is noticeably shorter than the Masoretic Text and differs in order, and both forms can be found at Qumran. Psalm 145 is an acrostic poem, and the Hebrew text lacks the verse beginning with the letter N. The Dead Sea Scrolls do have it, though some scholars think it was added later.

Our skeptical friends will say: Pastor, if the versions can change, how do you still dare to say God’s word hasn’t changed? Let me answer plainly. If someone taught you that “not one word was ever altered,” that statement really can’t stand, and the critics are right about it.

What do scholars think? Some stress that the line of transmission that became the Masoretic Text was very careful from early on. Others, like Eugene Ulrich, believe several literary versions existed side by side at the time and that the standard text took its fixed shape later. Evangelicals have traditionally distinguished the inspiration of the original manuscripts from the transmission of the copies: the copies have differences, and they can be checked against each other, and the content of the gospel does not hang on those differences. How best to describe the “original manuscripts” is still being discussed. We’re laying all of this out on the table, and we won’t pretend it has been solved.
Watch out for fakes and fake headlines

Two more cautions. First, who wrote these scrolls? The long-standing mainstream view is the Essenes or a related group, and some scholars argue they were a library from Jerusalem. There is no final verdict yet. Second, in 2020 the Museum of the Bible in the United States made public an independent report: all sixteen “Dead Sea Scroll” fragments in its collection were modern forgeries. The buyers were Christians, and they spent a great deal of money. A heart hungry for proof is exactly the forger’s market. The report didn’t shake the scrolls that were formally excavated, but it taught us a lesson: when we’re eager to defend God, that is when we need to keep our eyes wide open.

In 2025 there was more news, saying that AI had dated some scrolls earlier, even including a fragment of Daniel. The research is real and was published in a proper journal, but senior scholars also caution that this is just one more tool, and that we shouldn’t oversell it. When you see that kind of headline, friends, take a deep breath first, and forward it afterward.
Spiritual meaning: honesty is part of godliness

When ancient scribes checked their work stroke by stroke, that was a form of godliness. When we are willing today to look at differences, check evidence and refuse to forward things carelessly, that is the same godliness. A faith that fears being checked is really an anxious faith.
3. The grass has withered, the word remains
A scroll placed in a carpenter’s hands
Now let’s move the camera to Nazareth in the first century. One Sabbath, in the synagogue, someone hands a scroll of Isaiah to a man from a carpenter’s home.

The book of the prophet Isaiah was handed to him. He opened the book, and found the place where it was written, “The Spirit of the Lord is on me, because he has anointed me to preach good news to the poor. He has sent me to heal the broken hearted, to proclaim release to the captives, recovering of sight to the blind, to deliver those who are crushed, (Luke 4:17-18)

When He finished reading, He rolled up the scroll and said something that stopped the whole room cold: “Today, this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.” Brothers and sisters, the scroll in His hands belonged to the same world of copying as the Dead Sea Scrolls. Those nameless scribes could never have guessed that the words passing through their hands would one day be declared fulfilled by this Man’s own mouth.

The Great Isaiah Scroll also contains the Servant poem of chapter fifty-three. Jewish tradition and Christians read this passage differently, and we’ll talk about that in the next gallery. But at least one thing is certain: these words were already on parchment before Jesus was born. They are no after-the-fact creation of the church.
But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed. (Isaiah 53:5)
Spiritual meaning: this word is the gospel

The grass has withered. The scribes passed away, the Roman army came, the temple burned, and those parchment scrolls lay in the dark for nearly two thousand years. Yet Peter tells us that the word that endures is the very gospel preached to us.

For, “All flesh is like grass, and all of man’s glory like the flower in the grass. The grass withers, and its flower falls; but the Lord’s word endures forever.” This is the word of Good News which was preached to you. (1 Peter 1:24-25)
In the end our faith does not rest on a piece of parchment. It rests on the One the parchment bears witness to. He was pierced for us, and on the third day He rose again.

Today’s old notebook tells us three things. First, the main ingredients really haven’t drifted, and the overall stability is astonishing. Second, the differences are real too, and we say so plainly. Third, the One who handed all this down is a faithful God, and His word is finally fulfilled in Christ.

The 321 vision reminds us: the Bible is my standard, and a standard deserves serious study. The scribes of Qumran left almost no names behind. That is selflessness: they let God’s word be seen while they themselves disappeared from view. Do you have a ministry at church that you carry out quietly, one nobody knows about? Keep going, and let Jesus receive all the glory. Then lift your eyes from the temporary to the eternal. Empires and temples have all passed away. That thing keeping you awake tonight: how does it look against that length of time?

Let’s grow quiet together. Living God, people are like grass, yet Your word stands forever. Thank You for using so many nameless hands to bring Your word into ours. Help us to treasure this book and not to be afraid of facing hard questions honestly, because the Lord we believe in is the truth. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

1. When you heard that the Great Isaiah Scroll has more than twenty-six hundred variants, what was your first reaction? After looking at the overall consistency and the specific differences together, has your thinking changed?
2. What new understanding does the example of Goliath’s height give you of what “the Bible is reliable” means? How would you explain it to a child or a seeker?
3. What kind of service do the nameless scribes bring to mind? For whom are you willing to do something quietly this week?
New Testament Manuscripts: A Papyrus the Size of a Credit Card
Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away. (Matthew 24:35)

Brothers and sisters, peace to you! Please take out your wallet and pull out a credit card. Good, look at it. I want to introduce you to an elder about the same size. It lives in a library in Manchester, England, and its catalog number is P52. It is a scrap of papyrus bought in Egypt. A scholar bought it in an Egyptian market in 1920, and it was formally published only in 1935. What is copied on it is John chapter 18.

Think about it: it has come down from two thousand years ago, and all that is left is the size of a card, with a few lines of writing. If you had been the one to choose, you would probably have wanted John 3:16 to survive, wouldn’t you? What survived instead is this sentence:
Pilate said to him, “What is truth?” (John 18:38)

Every time I think about this, I feel God has a sense of humor. One of the most common challenges to the Bible around the world today is exactly this sentence: how do you know this book is true? It has been copied for thousands of years, so can it still be trusted? Today we will face that question. Let me say up front that I will not give you an answer so neat that it looks too good to be true. We will check three things: how many manuscripts we actually have, how serious the errors in them really are, and how far we can go once we have checked.
One: Be honest with the numbers, and honest with the dates

Many speakers used to say “over five thousand eight hundred Greek New Testament manuscripts.” In 2023, two scholars at the Institute for New Testament Textual Research in Münster, Germany, recounted the official catalog and arrived at a figure of about five thousand seven hundred entries; subtracting those that have been destroyed or whose whereabouts are unknown, about five thousand five hundred and forty-one. And please don’t imagine that these are five thousand complete New Testaments. Most of them are a passage, a few pages, a few books. Does a difference of a hundred matter to us? What matters is the attitude: if a witness pads even his arithmetic, people will not dare to listen to what comes after.

Why is this number so hard to count? Because some manuscripts are scattered across several countries, with one fragment in Dublin and the other half in Switzerland; and in some single artifacts people from different centuries each copied a section, so do you count one item or two? And what about amulets? The number is also still changing. CSNTM, an American institution that specializes in photographing manuscripts, reports that in the course of its work it has found nearly sixty previously unregistered manuscripts, which have been added to the official catalog. So when you hear a number, rather than memorizing it, ask: which year, and who counted?
How early is the earliest manuscript?

P52 is often said to date to AD 125. But its date can only be set by comparing handwriting, like looking at the script of an old letter and guessing in what year of the Republic it was written. The scholar Nongbri has written two papers pointing out that handwriting cannot be fixed that accurately, and that the reasonable range may need to extend to the later second century or even the third. Other scholars have proposed 125 to 175. So the more honest way to put it is: it is one of the earliest New Testament manuscripts, from around the second century, with the upper and lower limits still under discussion.

Next is P46, Paul’s letters from about AD 200, with eighty-six leaves surviving, some in Michigan in the United States and some in Dublin, Ireland. It places Hebrews right after Romans, which shows how readers of that time regarded the letter. Then there is the fourth-century Codex Sinaiticus, which contains the complete New Testament and has the Epistle of Barnabas and part of the Shepherd of Hermas after it. Tischendorf said he saw a basket of old parchment about to be used as fuel in the monastery. It is a thrilling story, but the monastery’s side has a different account of how the book left, and that is still disputed today.

Here is another story that makes you blush. In 2012, in a public debate with Ehrman, the evangelical scholar Wallace said that a fragment of Mark had been dated to the first century. The whole room was electrified, Christians spread the news, and I believe quite a few pulpits repeated it. Then in 2018 the fragment was formally published, and its date was the late second to early third century. What did Wallace do? He publicly apologized to Ehrman and to others, saying he should not have believed what others told him without checking.
Spiritual meaning: admitting a mistake is also a witness

Brothers and sisters, this apology increased my respect for Christian scholars. Our faith speaks of sinners saved by grace, so why pretend to be people who never make mistakes? The thing most to be feared in sharing the gospel is not having a question we cannot answer; it is saying one notch more than we know in order to win. Humility overcomes pride, and here it comes down to one sentence: I was wrong, and I am correcting it.
Two: Four hundred thousand errors, and then what?

Ehrman studied under Metzger, the master of New Testament textual criticism, and today he is an agnostic. In 2005 he wrote the bestseller Misquoting Jesus. In it he says the differences among the manuscripts outnumber the words of the New Testament. The Greek New Testament has roughly one hundred and thirty-eight thousand words, and he estimated the variants at two hundred to four hundred thousand. Brothers and sisters, I am telling you that this sentence is true. Gurry’s later research put it even higher: variants, not counting spelling, number about five hundred thousand.

Some of you heard that and felt your heart race. But the same study points out the key thing: this number mainly reflects how much copying was done. For example, if fifty classmates copy the same passage from the blackboard, together they will certainly make more mistakes than one person copying. The total of typos is frightening, but to know what the teacher originally wrote, you should in fact be thankful for fifty notebooks. If only one notebook were left in the whole world, that would be real trouble, because if it were wrong you would not know.
Look at the nature, not just the quantity

Wallace divides variants into four categories, which in simple terms means asking two questions: does this difference affect the meaning, and could it be the original reading? Many are spelling or word order, where translation shows no difference at all. Those that meet both conditions he estimates at about one percent. For example, in 1 John 1:4, is it our joy or your joy? That is well worth studying, but it will not affect your salvation.

Of course, there are harder ones. In Mark 1:41, most manuscripts say Jesus was moved with compassion and a few say Jesus was angry. Even Wallace leans toward thinking that “angry” may be the original. Would that change the portrait of Jesus? Look at the same book:

When he had looked around at them with anger, being grieved at the hardening of their hearts, he said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” He stretched it out, and his hand was restored as healthy as the other. (Mark 3:5)

Jesus was always capable of anger, and when He was angry He healed the man right then. Now look at the two best-known passages. Mark 16:9 to 20 is missing from both of the great manuscripts, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. The story of the woman caught in adultery in John is also missing from the early manuscripts; most scholars think it was not part of the original work, and quite a few think it may preserve a genuine story of Jesus. And there is 1 John 5:7 to 8, where some old English translations have an extra sentence that spells out the Trinity, which the Chinese Union Version does not; the manuscript evidence for that sentence is also very late. Wallace’s conclusion is that removing these passages would not change any basic doctrine. In an interview in the paperback edition, Ehrman also said that his position does not conflict with his teacher Metzger’s view that the essential beliefs of the faith are not affected by the variants. Still, he maintains that some variants do affect interpretation, and we should report that faithfully too.
Spiritual meaning: no need to give the Bible a facelift

Someone asks: Pastor, won’t talking about these things make believers stumble? I ask in return: if a person at thirty first discovers online that there is a problem with the ending of Mark, and thinks the church deliberately hid it from him, that is the person who will truly stumble. The Bible is my standard, and a standard is not afraid of being inspected. When you go home today and open your Bible and see in small print that some ancient manuscripts read this or that, that is your Bible telling you the truth.
Three: How far can the manuscripts take us?

We love competitions. Older books said the Iliad has only six hundred or so manuscripts. A more recent count has about one thousand seven hundred and fifty-seven, so the New Testament still has about three times as many, but the gap is not as lopsided as used to be claimed. The Roman historian Tacitus’s Annals basically depends on two medieval manuscripts. No one concludes from that that Tacitus cannot be read.

But please hear the most important sentence: many manuscripts do not mean the content is true. A forged invoice photocopied ten thousand times is still a forged invoice. Manuscript study answers the question of what the author originally wrote. Whether what he wrote is right, whether Jesus rose from the dead, is another question, to be checked by history and testimony, and in Jesus Hall we have a gallery devoted to it. What we can say with great confidence today is this: the New Testament in your hands, compared with what the authors wrote back then, is reliable enough for you to read it seriously; for the great majority of it we have very good grounds, and the few places that are uncertain we mark honestly.

Look at the fate of these manuscripts: thrown on rubbish heaps in Egypt, burned, eaten by worms, miscopied by copyists. When Paul himself wrote 2 Timothy, he too was locked in prison. And yet he said something with great spirit:
in which I suffer hardship to the point of chains as a criminal. But God’s word isn’t chained. (2 Timothy 2:9)
Spiritual meaning: the One who stood before Pilate

Back to that card. Pilate asked, “What is truth?” and walked out without waiting for the answer. He did not realize that the truth was standing before him in chains. In less than a day this Truth was nailed to a cross and died for our sins; on the third day He rose. God has always worked this way: He puts the treasure in clay jars, entrusts His word to hands that can miscopy, and places salvation in a condemned man. Letting Jesus receive all the glory includes this too: that so fragile a transmission has reached you today.

This week I ask you to do one small thing: read Mark 16, look at the seam between verse 8 and verse 9, and see how your Bible marks it. Then, the next time a friend says the Bible has been changed many times, don’t rush to counterattack. You can ask him: How do you think one could check to see how far that statement is right? That question may be the start of his first serious opening of this book. Don’t be like Pilate, who asked and walked away. Ask, and then wait a moment for the answer.

Lord Jesus, You are the truth. Thank You for passing Your word down through so many nameless hands, generation after generation, until it reached mine. Save me from exaggerated testimony, and save me also from the pride of suspicion; let me hear Your voice and follow You, because You died and rose for me. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

2. How do you feel about Wallace’s public apology? When sharing your faith, have you ever said one notch more than you knew in order to persuade someone?
3. How does the sentence “many manuscripts do not mean the content is true” help you and your unbelieving friends talk about the Bible more honestly?
How Was the Canon Formed? The Story of a Pharmacopoeia

knowing this first, that no prophecy of Scripture is of private interpretation. For no prophecy ever came by the will of man, but holy men of God spoke, being moved by the Holy Spirit. (2 Peter 1:20-21)

Brothers and sisters, peace to you! Has a friend ever asked you: isn’t your Bible just what the Roman emperor Constantine picked at a meeting? He kept what he liked and burned what he didn’t. This claim became even more popular after the novel The Da Vinci Code, and many people learn church history from movies.

There is even a more colorful version. In AD 325, at the Council of Nicaea, the bishops piled all the books on the altar, everyone prayed together, and the false books fell to the floor by themselves while the true ones stayed on top. My first thought when I heard this story was: if such a trick really existed, we could do away with pastors’ exams today.

Where does this story come from? It comes from a Greek document of about the ninth century, more than five hundred years after Nicaea. In 1764 the French thinker Voltaire told it as a joke in his Philosophical Dictionary, and it spread. When we check the records of the Council of Nicaea, and check what Eusebius and Athanasius, who were around at the time, wrote, nobody mentions that this council set the list of biblical books. Even Ehrman, who does not hold the Christian faith, says plainly that Constantine had nothing to do with the formation of the canon.

But, brothers and sisters, it would not be honest to have a laugh and move on. Because the next question is still there: if the emperor did not decide, then who did? How was it decided? Why these 66 books? Today let’s look.
One: Not an afternoon, but several hundred years
A rejected man forced the question

Around AD 140 a man named Marcion felt that the God of the Old Testament was not the same as the Father of Jesus, so he put together a Bible of his own: one gospel similar to Luke, plus ten letters of Paul, and nothing else. The church rejected him. But that rejection forced everyone to face a question: all right, then which books do we actually accept? It is a bit like an old bookcase at home that nobody pays attention to, until someone says most of the books should be thrown out, and the whole family sits down to discuss it.

Around AD 180, Irenaeus, the bishop of Lyon, said that the Gospels can be neither more nor fewer than four, because the world has four quarters and the winds have four directions. That argument sounds a bit charming today, but note the setting in which he wrote it: the four Gospels were already recognized by the church of the time. He was finding an illustration for an established fact.

In 1740 an Italian scholar, Muratori, found a damaged Latin list of books in a library in Milan. The manuscript itself is very late, and most scholars date the content to the late second century, though some argue for the fourth. It lists about 22 of today’s 27 books. One line is especially interesting: it recommends that people read the Shepherd of Hermas, but says that this book was written only recently and so cannot be read out in church as Scripture. Did you catch that? Their standard was not whether they liked the book, but whether it had a connection with the apostles.

Then over a hundred years went by. Around 330, Eusebius sorted books into three groups: recognized, disputed and rejected. James, Jude and 2 Peter were all in the disputed column. In 367 Athanasius wrote an Easter letter that lists exactly the same 27 books as today and says that in these alone the teaching of godliness is proclaimed. The regional councils of Hippo and Carthage later listed the same books.

Please note two small points. First, Athanasius is generally thought to be the earliest writer in the surviving literature to use the language of “canonized” for these books, which shows that even the use of the word “canon” took shape slowly. Second, his Old Testament list is not exactly the same as the Protestant one today: Esther is not in his canon, and he put it among the books that may be read by new believers. So even in 367 the matter was not settled in one stroke; Revelation still had a long wait before being generally accepted in some Eastern churches, and the Armenian Bible did not include it until around AD 1200.

So what standards did people of that time actually use? Scholars summarize them as three questions. First, does it have a connection with the apostles? However good the Shepherd of Hermas is, it came too late. Second, are churches in different places all using it? A book that is popular in only one city does not count. Third, does it agree with the gospel everyone received from the apostles? Marcion’s version, which threw out the God of the Old Testament, could not pass this test. These three questions are not a mathematical formula, and sometimes they pulled against one another, which is why the arguments went on so long. But you can see that this is a different matter from who held the most power and whom the emperor liked.
Spiritual meaning: a pharmacopoeia does not make the medicine work

Let me use an illustration. A pharmacopoeia lists which medicines work, but a medicine does not work because it was written into the pharmacopoeia. It was written down after generations of doctors and patients had used it. Christians believe that what the church did was to recognize, not to authorize. Of course, our friend can ask in return: who compiled the pharmacopoeia? Did the compilers have an agenda? That is a fair question. We will get to it in a moment.
My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me. (John 10:27)
Two: Don’t tell the story too cleanly
There were arguments, and we needn’t hide them

We shouldn’t tell this history as if it were all smooth sailing. Hebrews was hesitated over in the Western church for a time, and Revelation was questioned for a long time in the East. In the Peshitta, the Syriac church’s version, the New Testament originally had only 22 books, without 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John, Jude and Revelation. Luther also placed Hebrews, James, Jude and Revelation in a secondary position. And 2 Peter, where today’s theme passage comes from, was itself in the disputed column back then, and to this day scholars still discuss the question of its authorship.

Some books were also quite popular for a time. Codex Sinaiticus has the Shepherd of Hermas attached, and Athanasius himself said this book may be read by new believers but does not belong to the canon. So the process was not black and white, nor was it settled by a committee.

One school in the academy holds that the canon was a decision of the church in the third and fourth centuries, with the shadow of the power and theological struggles of the day on it. The Christian scholar Kruger holds that the sense of authority existed within Christianity much earlier: the apostles wrote with authority from the start, and the letters circulated among the churches. I think both sides have something to acknowledge: the church did exercise judgment, and the judgment did take a long time. As a believer, I trust that God was in control throughout this process, but that is a judgment of faith, and the historical sources cannot give me a guarantee on it.
The Gospel of Thomas and the Gospel of Judas

What about the so-called lost gospels? The Gospel of Thomas has 114 sayings, and a complete Coptic text came to light in Egypt in 1945. Scholars have no consensus on when it was written; some think it preserves early tradition, and we should respect that discussion. But its form is only a list of sayings, and it contains no narrative of the suffering and resurrection. The manuscript of the Gospel of Judas has been radiocarbon dated to between 220 and 340, Irenaeus mentioned it around 180, and scholars think it was probably composed in the second century. Levine, who took part in the study, said it gives us no new historical information about Jesus or Judas. They are valuable documents for studying the variety of early Christianity, but they are not a truth hidden away by an emperor.
Spiritual meaning: speaking humbly about the Apocrypha

As for the Old Testament, brothers and sisters in the Lord also differ. Protestants follow the 39 books of the Hebrew Bible, the Catholic Church confirmed the second canon at the Council of Trent in 1546, and the Orthodox list has a few more. Brothers and sisters, this is a family disagreeing about the bookcase. We can explain our reasons clearly and respectfully, and we do not have to treat the others as enemies. Letting God be God and people be people.

Let me also mention a mistake we ourselves often made. Many books used to say that around AD 90 the Jews held a council at Jamnia and fixed the Hebrew canon. That claim came from nineteenth-century scholars and circulated for a hundred years, until in 1964 Lewis and others went back to the sources and found that the evidence was very thin, and today most scholars no longer say it. Did you notice? This is the same flaw as the story of Nicaea: people love one meeting, one afternoon, one decision, because it makes the story easier to tell. History is usually slower.
Three: At the center of the list is a person
The most important reason Christians believe the Old Testament is that Jesus believed it. After His resurrection, He said this to His disciples:

He said to them, “This is what I told you while I was still with you, that all things which are written in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms concerning me must be fulfilled.” (Luke 24:44)

Look at this phrase: concerning me. The focus of the canon is not the bookcase but the Owner of the bookcase. He also told the disciples beforehand that the Holy Spirit would remind them of everything He had said. The church asked: Is this book from the apostles? Are churches everywhere reading it? Does it agree with the gospel that was handed down? In the end they were all asking one and the same thing: is this the voice of the Lord who was crucified and rose again?
Spiritual meaning: let the measuring rod measure me

The original meaning of canon is a measuring rod. We often use it to measure other people: you see, this brother is not in line with the Bible. But the rod must first be used to measure me. And we are often like Marcion, putting together a private edition of the Bible: highlighting the passages we like and turning past the ones we don’t. We keep the comforting ones and skip the ones that ask me to forgive. Moving from self-centered to selfless sometimes begins right here: let me read the passage I don’t want to read, and let Jesus reign in my bookcase.

Today we have seen that the Bible was not settled in one afternoon or by one emperor. It went through several hundred years, with arguments, with waiting, and with the reading aloud of many nameless believers generation after generation. The next time a friend asks you this, don’t rush to debate. You can ask him: What ancient sources do you think one would need to check to find out whether that claim is right? And this week, please pick a short letter you have never finished, Philemon or Jude, and read it through in one sitting.

Heavenly Father, thank You for opening Your mouth to speak to people, and for speaking Your last and deepest word through Your Son. Thank You for keeping Your church through the long course of history. Holy Spirit, open my ears so that I recognize the voice of the Good Shepherd, obey Your word, and let Jesus reign in my life. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

2. Hearing that there were so many arguments over the canon, do you feel uneasy or settled? Why?

Archaeology and the Old Testament: What the Spade Can Reach, and What It Can’t
Truth springs out of the earth. Righteousness has looked down from heaven. (Psalm 85:11)

Brothers and sisters, peace to you! Suppose one day your enemy set up a monument about you, covered from top to bottom with how he beat you. You probably wouldn’t be pleased. But three thousand years later, the very reason the world knows your family ever existed is your enemy’s monument. That is exactly what happened to the house of David.

Today we walk into the archaeology gallery of the Bible Hall. Let’s agree on the ground rules first. We haven’t come to hire bodyguards for the Bible, and we haven’t come to brag. What has been dug up, we will report as it stands, and what hasn’t been dug up, we will report as it stands too. A faith that can only stay on its feet by exaggerating isn’t worth believing.
Truth springs out of the earth. Righteousness has looked down from heaven. (Psalm 85:11)
The psalmist probably wasn’t thinking about archaeology, and yet his words fit so well today: some truthful testimony really does spring out of the earth.

In July 1993, at Tel Dan in northern Israel, a member of the archaeological team noticed a piece of basalt in the rubble with writing on it. The next year two more pieces were found. The text is in Aramaic, and most scholars think it comes from the time of Hazael, king of Damascus, which means the 9th century BC.

The man who raised it is full of himself. He says he defeated the king of Israel, and then defeated the king of a certain family. That word is written BYTDWD, and most scholars read it as “House of David.” Now notice this. Before the discovery, one school of scholars suspected that David was only a legend, the way we think about King Arthur. This stele wasn’t put up by the church. It was put up by an enemy, and it treats the “House of David” as a dynasty everybody knew about.

Of course, we have to be clear. That word has no word divider in the middle, and some scholars have proposed other readings. Others say that even if we read it as House of David, it can’t confirm David’s life story. We need to listen to all these objections. Most scholars still accept the reading. What it shows is this: by the 9th century BC there was a dynasty named after David. It hasn’t proved for you that David killed Goliath.
Two sides of the story: the Mesha Stele and Sennacherib

Let’s look at another stone. In 1868 a missionary saw a black stele at Dibon, in today’s Jordan. Later the local people smashed it to pieces. Thankfully, someone had already taken a paper impression, so the stele could be pieced back together, and today it sits in the Louvre. Its author is Mesha, king of Moab, the very man in the third chapter of 2 Kings.

Now Mesha king of Moab was a sheep breeder; and he supplied the king of Israel with one hundred thousand lambs and the wool of one hundred thousand rams. But when Ahab was dead, the king of Moab rebelled against the king of Israel. (2 Kings 3:4-5)

Mesha also mentions the house of Omri oppressing Moab, and he too tells of his revolt. But in his telling, he wins and his god Chemosh triumphs, while in 2 Kings the story ends rather differently. Friends, that’s perfectly normal. Two sets of fans can tell you about the same ball game and even give you different versions of the score, but nobody doubts the game was played.

Further on, in 701 BC, the Assyrian king Sennacherib attacked Judah. Back in Nineveh he covered his palace walls with scenes of the capture of Lachish: the siege ramps, the torches, the captured people. Today you can go to the British Museum and see them with your own eyes. His annals go on to say that he took 46 of Hezekiah’s fortified cities and shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem like a bird in a cage.

Here’s where it gets interesting. A great emperor carved a wall this enormous to boast about Lachish, and yet his annals don’t say he took Jerusalem. The Bible also records Hezekiah bowing his head and paying tribute, with no cover-up for its own king, and then records the Assyrians breaking camp and going home. The details on the two sides aren’t entirely the same, but the skeleton lines up. As for the great disaster in the camp recorded in 2 Kings, the Assyrian inscriptions don’t mention it. That is no surprise in victory propaganda, but it also means historians can’t get confirmation from the Assyrian side. So that’s just how we’ll tell it.
Spiritual meaning: God isn’t afraid of being checked

Brothers and sisters, look at the way the Bible is written. It lays kings’ names, place names and years out on the table, and it writes in the failures of its own kings. If all you wanted was an inspirational story, you wouldn’t make that kind of trouble for yourself. The God we believe in is a God who acts in real time and real space. He doesn’t need us to put makeup on Him.
2. The Hardest Question: We Won’t Take a Detour

Having come this far, if I told you only the good news, I would be deceiving you. Friends who are exploring the faith will go online and see it right away: there is no archaeological evidence for the Exodus. How much of that sentence is true?

Here is the part that’s true. To this day, Egyptian records make no direct mention of a great crowd of Israelites leaving, and the wilderness has left no agreed remains. The earliest Egyptian writing that mentions Israel is the Merneptah Stele, discovered in 1896 and dated around 1208 BC, which says Israel was already in the land of Canaan. It can tell us that Israel was there. It doesn’t tell us how they got there.

Jericho is the same. Kathleen Kenyon dated the destruction layer of the walls she dug up to about 1550 BC, earlier than the time usually pictured for Joshua. In 1990 Bryant Wood argued it should be moved to about 1400 BC, and scholars immediately answered him. Then the carbon dating results of 1995 landed closer to Kenyon.

So what do scholars say? There are two ends. At one end are the Egyptologist Kenneth Kitchen and James Hoffmeier, who hold that the Bible’s background details fit the ancient world and that a lack of direct evidence isn’t counterevidence. At the other end are Israel Finkelstein and Neil Silberman, who argue that no trace can be found of a mass departure and a rapid conquest, and that early Israel developed mainly from within Canaan itself. In between, quite a few people think a smaller group went through an escape from Egypt. Among evangelicals there are also differing views favoring an earlier or a later date. We set these side by side and don’t rule between them.

Let me say this to my Christian friends: this question hasn’t been settled. If someone tells you archaeology has completely confirmed the Exodus, please don’t forward it. In the same way, saying it has been completely refuted claims too much. Archaeology is like an old newspaper with most of it torn away. The parts you can read are precious, and the blank parts shouldn’t be hurriedly filled in.
Spiritual meaning: honesty is part of our witness

A brother said to me, “Pastor, when you talk about these things, aren’t you afraid people’s faith will be shaken?” I’m actually more afraid of something else: a child who has only ever heard “archaeology confirms it all” in Sunday school, then gets to college, reads the first article on the other side, and collapses completely. When we tell them honestly that the hard questions are still there, they won’t come to think later on that the church lied to them.
Faith doesn’t mean closing your eyes. It means keeping your eyes open and putting the questions still unsolved into the hands of a Lord you can trust.
3. The Blessing on a Tiny Silver Scroll

Finally, I want to take you to the smallest exhibit in the whole gallery. In 1979 Professor Gabriel Barkay was excavating burial chambers at Ketef Hinnom, southwest of Jerusalem. While cleaning up, a thirteen-year-old volunteer happened upon a storage pit that had never been robbed. Inside were two extremely tiny silver scrolls, and the larger one, when unrolled, was less than ten centimeters long.

Later they were studied again using new imaging technology, published in 2004. What could be read turned out to be the priestly blessing from the sixth chapter of Numbers. The date is around 600 BC, several hundred years earlier than the Dead Sea Scrolls, and they are the oldest fragments of Old Testament text we know of so far.
Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace. (Numbers 6:24-26)

Once again I have to tap the brakes. These two tiny silver scrolls can tell us that this blessing was already circulating at that time. They aren’t enough to show that the whole book of Numbers had been completed by then, and a minority of scholars question the date. You see what a killjoy I am, friends! And yet this makes it all the more moving: a person in Jerusalem hung these few lines around his neck, and then the armies of Babylon came.
Spiritual meaning: His face shines on us in Christ

Jerusalem fell, and that person was probably gone too, but the blessing did not end. God had promised that the house of David would stand firm forever. Later the throne was cut off, and it looked as if the promise had come to nothing. Hundreds of years on, a carpenter’s son was born in the city of David, was nailed to a Roman cross, and on the third day rose from the dead.

He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. The Lord God will give him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever. There will be no end to his Kingdom. (Luke 1:32-33)

The enemy on the Tel Dan Stele thought the house of David was finished, and yet it was his stele that broke and got built into a wall. The line “Yahweh make his face to shine on you” found its deepest fulfillment in Jesus. He carried our sins in our place, so the face of God no longer makes us afraid, and we can come face to face with Him and receive peace. Paul says that the glory of God is shown in the face of Jesus Christ.

That isn’t something archaeology can dig up. A spade can reach a stele, but it can’t reach the meaning of the resurrection. Archaeology helps us confirm that the stage is real. Who the main character is, you only see in the gospel.

Brothers and sisters, take three sentences home with you today. First, the Bible is a book that dares to be checked, and many of its names and places have testimony from the ground. Second, some questions don’t have answers yet, and we say so honestly. Third, archaeology can’t take the place of faith; our trust rests on the faithful Lord.

To say it the 321 way: the Bible is my standard, so I won’t exaggerate on its behalf, and I won’t give it a discount either. Humility overcomes pride, so I don’t have to win every debate, and I can let God be God. The empires’ steles have all broken. So move from a temporary perspective to an eternal one: the thing you can’t put down today, if you set it against that long a span of time, wouldn’t it look different? This week, find someone and read this blessing over them. When one person can ask God’s face to shine on another, that is already building God’s kingdom system.

Please quiet your hearts with me. Faithful God, thank You for acting in real history and fulfilling Your promises in the Lord Jesus. We have so many questions not yet solved. Today we won’t pretend, and we won’t be afraid; we hand them all over to You. Please make Your face to shine on us, be gracious to us, and give us peace. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
1. Which moved you most: the “House of David” on the enemy’s stele, or the blessing on the silver scroll? Why?
2. Have you ever heard “archaeology completely confirms the Bible” or “archaeology has overturned the Bible”? After today, how would you respond to each of these claims?
3. Whom do you want to read the blessing of Numbers 6:24-26 over this week? At our next meeting, share how they responded and how you felt.
Archaeology and the New Testament: The Nail in the Heel Bone

it seemed good to me also, having traced the course of all things accurately from the first, to write to you in order, most excellent Theophilus; that you might know the certainty concerning the things in which you were instructed. (Luke 1:3-4)

Brothers and sisters, peace to you! In 1968, at a building site north of Jerusalem, construction workers were digging foundations when they broke into several ancient Jewish burial caves. Archaeologists hurried over and opened one of the stone boxes that held bones. A name was carved on it: Yehohanan. Inside was a human heel bone with an iron nail through it, about eleven and a half centimeters long.

Please think about that picture. A man from two thousand years ago, with the nail still in his bone. Before this we knew the Romans crucified people, and ancient writings say a great deal about it, but of the actual bones of a crucified person, archaeology had almost none. For the first time, this was not just words. It was a bone you could hold in your hand.

Today we walk into the Bible Hall to look at archaeology and the New Testament. Let me state my position first: archaeology is very useful, but it has limits. We will look at three things: the names carved in stone, the places found in the ground, and the one thing stones cannot say. The opening words of Luke are our starting point today:

Since many have undertaken to set in order a narrative concerning those matters which have been fulfilled among us, even as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and servants of the word delivered them to us, (Luke 1:1-2)

In June 1961, at Caesarea on the Israeli coast, an Italian archaeological team found a stone in the ancient theater, about eighty-two centimeters tall. Later people had taken it and used it as a step, so a monument from the age of the emperors ended up being walked on for centuries. The writing on it is damaged, but after reconstruction it has the name of Pilate and his title: prefect of Judea.

Let me first correct something you often hear. Some say that before this stone was dug up, scholars doubted that Pilate had ever existed. Friends, that is not accurate. Josephus, Philo and Tacitus had already written about him. So what is the value of this stone? It was carved by people of that time, and it preserves the title he held then. We don’t need to exaggerate; it is exciting enough.

In 1990, while a park was being built south of Jerusalem, a bulldozer opened the roof of an ancient tomb. Inside was an exquisitely made bone box, with a name carved on it twice, meaning Joseph son of Caiaphas. Josephus tells us that the high priest who questioned Jesus had the full name Joseph Caiaphas. In the box were the bones of a man of about sixty. When we think of the man in the Gospels who tore his clothes and condemned Jesus to death, and that his bones may be right here, doesn’t something stir in you?

But we must add: some scholars have raised questions, for example that the spelling is not exactly what one would expect and the box has no title of high priest. Most scholars accept the identification, so we say: very possibly, but we do not say certainly.

The third name is less famous. At Delphi in Greece, nine fragments were found that fit together into a letter from the Roman emperor Claudius, written around AD 52, mentioning the proconsul Gallio. Turn to Acts chapter 18: Paul has been dragged into court in Corinth, and the official sitting on the bench is this man. The significance is very practical: Paul’s whole life chronology can be worked out only with fixed points like this. An imperial letter about other business, without meaning to, drove a nail of time into the book of Acts.
But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews with one accord rose up against Paul and brought him before the judgment seat, (Acts 18:12)
Spiritual meaning: a Savior nailed into the timeline

For two thousand years the church has said one line in its creed: that Jesus suffered under Pontius Pilate. Have you ever wondered why a Roman official’s name is in the creed? Because this event has a date that can be checked. Luke is the same: he fixes events in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, in the term of Pilate. Many ancient stories begin “once upon a time,” but the Gospels hand over a record with a time and a place, for people to check. The truth is not afraid of being checked.
A pool found while fixing a sewer

In the autumn of 2004, in the City of David area of Jerusalem, workers repairing a sewer scraped into stone steps. The archaeologists Shukron and Reich took one look and saw that this was a large pool from the Second Temple period, nearly seventy meters wide, with coins from that era in the plaster. The small pool that people used to take tourists to see turns out, as we see it today, to be a building left from the fifth century. This large pool was thought to be the Pool of Siloam of John chapter 9.
and said to him, “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam” (which means “Sent”). So he went away, washed, and came back seeing. (John 9:7)

But in 2023, an Israeli archaeologist, Szanton, published a paper arguing that the true Pool of Siloam may be at the site of another pool a few hundred feet to the north, which can be dated to the early Roman period. And new excavations since 2022 have pushed the date of a large dam in this area back to about 800 BC. I like these developments. They remind us that archaeology is not settled once and for all; it is work that keeps being revised. Whichever pool it turns out to be, there really were large pools like this at the southern end of first-century Jerusalem, and John was not writing about an imaginary place.

Now Bethesda. John chapter 5 says there was a pool near the Sheep Gate with five porticoes, where many sick people lay. In the nineteenth century scholars found large pools around the Church of St. Anne, and the 1964 excavation saw two large pools with a dividing wall between them and the remains of a Roman healing sanctuary nearby. So there is a little more background for why these sick people waited here. How the five porticoes were arranged is still discussed by scholars.

A certain man was there who had been sick for thirty-eight years. When Jesus saw him lying there, and knew that he had been sick for a long time, he asked him, “Do you want to be made well?” (John 5:5-6)

And then there is Nazareth. In December 2009, beside the Church of the Annunciation, the Israel Antiquities Authority found a small house from around the first century: two rooms, a courtyard, a cistern cut into the rock, and fragments of the limestone vessels that Jews commonly used. There was very little in it, and it was very plain. Later the British scholar Dark also studied a house beneath the nearby convent. Some ask: is this Jesus’ home? To be honest, there is no evidence at all. But what moves me is that the poverty of that village is plain to see.
Nathanael said to him, “Can any good thing come out of Nazareth?” Philip said to him, “Come and see.” (John 1:46)

Philip did not argue with Nathanael. He said: Come and see. This is the tone we should have when we share the gospel. What archaeology gives us is the footing for those words. We don’t have to overstate; we only have to say: the places in this book are real, the people are real, come and see.
Three: The one thing stones cannot say
Evidence we do not use, however moving

In 2002, a bone box caused a worldwide sensation, with an inscription that read: James, son of Joseph, brother of Jesus. If it were genuine, what news that would be! But the Israel Antiquities Authority soon accused someone of forging part of the writing. The case dragged on until 2012, when the judge found the defendants not guilty of forgery, but he also stated plainly that this did not mean the inscription is genuine, and that only the future can tell us. So, friends, however much we would like to use it, this bone box is not on our list of evidence. A moving but doubtful piece of evidence, once used, can destroy all our other testimony.
Archaeology stops at the door of the tomb

We also have to ask the hardest question. Add all of this together: can it prove that Jesus rose from the dead? No. A historical novel can also get its streets exactly right. A scholar who does not believe can fully accept the Pilate Stone and still not believe in Jesus. That is fair. What archaeology can rule out is the simple view that this is a fictional myth. It brings us to the door of the empty tomb, and then you have to decide for yourself whether to walk in.

Let’s return to Yehohanan. Early reports said both his feet were pierced by one nail and that his arms were nailed too. In 1985 two scholars reexamined the bones and corrected this: there was only one heel bone, and the arms may have been tied. Later there was also an Italian case published in 2018, with a perforation but no nail, and the researchers themselves say only that it is possible. Another thing worth noticing: Yehohanan was buried in a Jewish family tomb, and his bones were gathered into a bone box. This at least shows that crucified people were not always simply thrown away, though of course one case cannot testify to Jesus’ tomb. These are details, and one thing has not changed: that nail is real. Thomas said: Unless I see in his hands the print of the nails, I will not believe. How did Jesus answer him afterward?
Then he said to Thomas, “Reach here your finger, and see my hands. Reach here your hand, and put it into my side. Don’t be unbelieving, but believing.” (John 20:27)
Spiritual meaning: the marks of the nails on a living man

Yehohanan’s nail stayed in the bone, and the bone stayed in the tomb. The disciples said the marks of Jesus’ nails were on the hands of a living man. This is the biggest difference between the two, and it is the whole of the gospel. Isaiah had already said it: he was pierced for our transgressions, he was crushed for our iniquities. Friends, a museum can keep a heel bone, but it cannot keep a hand that is stretched out to you.

Today we have seen that stones can testify for the Gospels, up to a certain point. People will not read the archaeology reports; they look at you and me. Life first, then relationships, then ministry: our lives are a testimony that can be checked. The blind man in John chapter 9 had no degree in archaeology either; he said just one sentence: though I was blind, now I see. This week please read that chapter, then write down one sentence of your own about what you were before and what you are now, and tell one person. If a friend is willing to talk, ask him: If the place names and official titles in an ancient book are repeatedly dug up and found to match, would that make you more willing to read it? What other tests does it still have to pass?

Lord Jesus, You did not live in a myth. You entered our history, walked our streets, and suffered a real nailing. Thank You for being pierced for my sins and for rising from the dead. Move me from only wanting to see evidence to saying to You: My Lord and my God. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
1. Which archaeological find today moved you most? How far do you think it can support the faith, and where does it stop?
2. How does the practice of not using the James ossuary, “however moving,” speak to the way you share your faith?
3. What is your “once… now…”? Please share it in two minutes.
Messianic Prophecy: A Key Older Than Jesus

He said to them, “This is what I told you while I was still with you, that all things which are written in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms concerning me must be fulfilled.” (Luke 24:44)

Brothers and sisters, peace to you! Suppose that in the old desk your grandfather left behind, you find a rusty key. You take it to an old locksmith, and he squints at it and says, “This key is a hundred years old at the very least.”

Very good, the key is old enough. But let me ask you, which door does it open? The old craftsman can’t tell you. You have to carry it from door to door and try each one. And even if one door does open, someone standing nearby may still ask: wasn’t this door frame shaved down later, just to match this key?

Today, as we talk about messianic prophecy, this key is exactly what we’re talking about. When many people hear the word prophecy, they think of those charts on the internet: Jesus fulfilled three hundred prophecies, the odds are a hundred million times lower than winning the lottery, believe it or not. Today I want to say something that may surprise you: those numbers, we don’t use. We’re going to take a slower, more honest and more moving road, and it will bring us before the same Jesus.
1. The key is old enough: Isaiah 53 was written before Jesus
Leather scrolls in a cave by the Dead Sea

Among the Dead Sea Scrolls there is a scroll of Isaiah called the Great Isaiah Scroll. It is about seven point three meters long, a full fifty-four columns, complete from beginning to end. From the handwriting, experts judge that it was copied somewhere around 150 BC to 100 BC; the calibrated carbon-dating range runs from 356 BC to 103 BC.
In other words, before Mary was even born, chapter 53 was already lying on this leather scroll. No one can say this passage was added by Christians after the fact to fit Jesus.

We also have to be honest. This scroll has more than two thousand six hundred variants, large and small, against the later Masoretic manuscripts. Most concern spelling and word order, and some involve whole sentences. At chapter 53, verse 11, it has an added word, “light,” and the Septuagint has it too. Overall they are very close, and in the details they differ. We say so plainly, and there is not a single word we need to cover up for it.
What this means for us spiritually: God isn’t afraid of your checking

Friends, a faith built on a box no one dares to open is a very fragile thing. God allowed these scrolls to lie in a cave for two thousand years, and He allows today’s scholars to examine them with magnifying glasses and with carbon-14. His word stands up to checking. You can check it too.
He was despised and rejected by men, a man of suffering and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him. (Isaiah 53:3)
2. Which door? First hear out how our Jewish brothers read it
Don’t draw conclusions for someone else’s tradition

For this next part, I’d like to ask everyone to slow down. When we Christians read this passage, we immediately think of the cross. But in the Jewish tradition of reading Scripture, this road runs in more than one direction.

The great eleventh-century French rabbi Rashi said that this prophet habitually addresses all Israel as one person, so the one despised, the one from whom faces are hidden, is the whole nation. Some Christians have claimed that Rashi invented this to oppose Christianity. That claim doesn’t hold up. Around AD 248, the Christian scholar Origen himself recorded that a Jewish scholar debated with him and said this passage referred to the whole nation. A Christian’s own record, eight hundred years earlier than Rashi.

On the other side, some people say Jews have never connected this passage with the Messiah, and that’s wrong too. The Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and paraphrase, reads at 52:13 “my servant the Messiah.” The Babylonian Talmud’s tractate Sanhedrin, discussing the names of the Messiah, also cites 53:4. So what we have is a rich map with more than a one-way street on it.

Brothers and sisters, one more heavy thing needs adding. Please picture an elderly Jewish man whose family in Europe was driven out and burned out, often by people marching under the banner of the cross. He reads “He was despised and rejected by men,” and he thinks of his grandparents. If you walk straight up to him and say, “You’ve all read this wrong!” what kind of attitude is that? When we share the gospel, we must come with a repentant heart and with respect for this pain.
Why Christians read it as Jesus

Having shown that respect, we can also calmly explain our own reasons. 53:8 says the servant was cut off “for the disobedience of my people,” and here the servant and “my people” look like two parties. The servant of Isaiah 49 is to bring Jacob back to God, and doesn’t appear to be Jacob himself. And this servant endures in silence, with no violence and no deceit. The prophets’ books never describe their own nation that way; in fact they often rebuke her severely.

A Jewish friend will answer: the book of Isaiah calls Israel “my servant” again and again, so how can you skip over that? That’s a real point too. Both sides have Scripture. We lay them side by side here and invite you to open it and read for yourself.
The king on a donkey, and an argument over one word

Then there is Zechariah 9:9, the king who comes “lowly, and riding on a donkey.” In the Talmud a certain Rabbi Alexandri said that if Israel is worthy, the Messiah will come on the clouds of heaven, and if unworthy, riding on a donkey. You see, the ancient rabbis themselves were pondering this contradiction: how could a king ride a donkey?

Jesus deliberately chose a donkey to enter the city, so a skeptical friend will say, “What’s so remarkable about that? He was acting it out.” That’s half right. But let me ask: someone playing the Messiah ought to be after royal power and glory. If he acts it out and the final scene is crucifixion, what was the show for?

Psalm 22:16 is another example. The Chinese Union Version, like the World English Bible, reads “They have pierced my hands and feet.” The Masoretic Text, though, has “like a lion, my hands and my feet.” The Septuagint has a verb, and a fragment from Nahal Hever seems to support the verb too, but the handwriting is blurred and the root is disputed. Jewish scholars and Christian scholars are still writing articles on both sides. My advice: don’t press your faith down onto this one word. The New Testament quotes several verses of Psalm 22, and it doesn’t quote this one either.
What this means for us spiritually: sincere readers of Scripture respect one another

So, friends, the next time you hear someone say, “The Jews’ own Bible spells it all out clearly, and they refuse to believe on purpose,” please don’t applaud. That statement is unfair, and it isn’t true. Paul himself said the cross is a stumbling block to Jews. It is a real stone, and we ourselves only got past it because the Holy Spirit opened our eyes. We have nothing to be proud of.
but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Greeks, (1 Corinthians 1:23)
3. When the door opens: the cross becomes my grace

Now back to that probability chart. In 1958 an American teacher named Stoner wrote a book estimating that the probability of one man fulfilling eight prophecies is 1 in 10 to the 17th power. That number has traveled around the world.

But try it out and it leaks. First, each probability is an estimate. You guess one in a hundred, I guess one in a thousand; it all comes down to feel. Second, the eight are multiplied as though they had nothing to do with one another, when they are actually linked. It’s like calculating the odds of someone both “being able to swim” and “being able to dive” by multiplying the two numbers, which makes the person look far rarer than he is. Third, some of these are things a person can deliberately carry out. Fourth, the eight were picked after the fact. Critics have pointed out these problems, and they are right. We thank them.
Faith doesn’t need padded numbers. Pad one place, and your friends will suspect you padded all the rest too.

It is this: once the key opens the door, what’s inside is completely unexpected. First-century Jews hoped for a king. They hoped for their nation restored, and for the Romans driven out, a perfectly reasonable hope. When the second-century Jew Trypho debated with the Christian Justin, what he could least get past was this: how could the Messiah hang on a tree under a curse?
