The disciples themselves couldn’t make the turn. John honestly records that the disciples didn’t understand these things at first, and that only when Jesus was glorified did they remember. They didn’t first have a script for a dying Messiah and then go looking for an actor. They were knocked flat by the cross and the empty tomb, and only then did they go back and reread the Scriptures and discover that the answer had been there all along.

It’s as if you had known a friend for thirty years, and after he passed away his family handed you a diary. You open it, and only then do you learn that all those actions you once found baffling, he did one by one for you. That is how the hearts of those two on the Emmaus road caught fire.
Beginning from Moses and from all the prophets, he explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself. (Luke 24:27)
What this means for us spiritually: let Jesus reign, the King who rides a donkey

Brothers and sisters, all of us in our hearts are also hoping for the King on the warhorse. Lord, deal with my boss for me, turn the situation around for me, let me win it all back. But this King rode into the city on a donkey and walked all the way to the cross.

His reign begins with bearing my sins. Peter writes, “He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree.” So we turn from being self-centered, from “I have to win, I have to be right,” toward selflessness. At home, argue one fewer line about who’s right. At church, let someone else stand up front. Let Jesus receive all the glory, and it starts in small places like these.
He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we, having died to sins, might live to righteousness. You were healed by his wounds. (1 Peter 2:24)

Today we haven’t used a single startling number. We’ve only said a few things. The key is indeed old enough: the text is older than Jesus. Which door it opens depends on interpretation; Jewish tradition has its reasons, and we ought to respect them. And Christians see that behind the door this key opens stands a Lord who was wounded for us.

As for how to count Daniel’s seventy weeks, our evangelical forebears held differing views. We won’t rule among them, and we certainly won’t use it to calculate dates. The Lord’s return calls for watchful waiting, and there’s no need to punch a calculator.

If you are still searching, you’re welcome to bring your questions, open Isaiah 53 and read it through. Maybe you can’t yet be sure who it refers to, and that’s all right. When Philip met the eunuch, this was the eunuch’s question too: “Who is the prophet talking about?” An honest question is a very good place to start.

Faithful Lord, from ancient times until now Your word has never failed. Thank You for being pierced for my transgressions and crushed for my iniquities. Forgive us for the times we have used Your word to hurt others, and forgive us for wanting only the King on the warhorse. Make our hearts burn for Your word, and give us gentleness to respect those who read it differently from us. In the name of Jesus, amen.

1. “The key is old enough” and “it opens this door” are two different questions. When you heard about prophecy in the past, did you mix the two together? How does this distinction help you share the gospel?
2. Imagine you have a Jewish friend who tells you that Isaiah 53 is the scar of his people. How would you listen and respond?
3. Lately, what has your heart been hoping for, “the King on the warhorse” or “the King on the donkey”? In which relationship could you practice letting go of the need to win this week?
The Historical Details of Acts: A Stone from a City Gate

But he said, “I am not crazy, most excellent Festus, but boldly declare words of truth and reasonableness. For the king knows of these things, to whom also I speak freely. For I am persuaded that none of these things is hidden from him, for this has not been done in a corner. (Acts 26:25-26)

Brothers and sisters, peace to you! Has anyone here ever had a teacher catch a wrong character in your essay? Now imagine this: an author writes a book, and in it he uses an official title. Later readers search through every Greek text they have and cannot find that word anywhere. So they say: this author must have gotten it wrong. He had no idea what he was writing about.

That author is Luke, and the title is the Greek word politarchēs, the “rulers of the city” in Acts 17. And what happened? In Thessalonica, in Greece, there was an ancient city gate called the Vardar Gate, which was torn down in 1876. On one of the stones taken from it, this very title was carved in plain letters. That stone sits in the British Museum today. Since then several more inscriptions have come to light, most of them in the region of Macedonia.

Hearing this, some of you want to slap the table and say: See! The Bible is completely right! Hold on, please. Today we are going to do something harder than slapping the table. We will check carefully where Luke is right, lay out the places that remain unsolved, and then ask what all this really means for you and me.
1. How well did Luke do his homework?

Right at the start Luke tells us his working method. He has traced the course of all things accurately from the first, and he writes to Theophilus in order. This was a common opening for the authors of histories in that day.

it seemed good to me also, having traced the course of all things accurately from the first, to write to you in order, most excellent Theophilus; that you might know the certainty concerning the things in which you were instructed. (Luke 1:3-4)

How do we know whether someone’s travel story is true? We listen to the small things. If he tells you, that beef noodle shop is closed on Mondays, the owner’s wife is left-handed, and you have to circle around the one-way street at the end of the alley, you will probably believe he really went. Luke has this kind of “closed on Mondays” detail too.

Take the city officials of Thessalonica. The inscriptions say the city had five of them in the time of Augustus, and Luke uses exactly the plural. Cyprus was a senatorial province governed by a proconsul, and Luke calls Sergius Paulus a proconsul. Then there is Gallio in Corinth: at Delphi a letter from the emperor Claudius was unearthed, from around AD 52, and it mentions the proconsul Gallio, which has become a key anchor point for building Paul’s chronology. As for Felix and Drusilla, Festus and Ananias, all of them can be set beside the Jewish historian Josephus.
A few more titles to check

Let’s look at a few more examples, and practice checking along the way. When Paul came ashore on Malta, the man who hosted him is called, in the English Bible, the chief man of the island. The Greek simply says “the first man.” That sounds casual, as if it were just pointing to the most respected person in the village. But two inscriptions from Malta (one Greek, from the early first century, calling a man “first of the Maltese”; one Latin, from the second century) use the same kind of expression, which scholars generally read as an official-sounding title, though they disagree on whether it was an office or an honor. Luke does not give him an impressive Roman office. He uses what the locals called him. Ramsay even guessed that Publius was his Roman name, that the villagers simply called him by it, and that Luke wrote it down as he heard it. This is only a guess, and we should not take it too seriously, but it is a vivid picture.
Now in the neighborhood of that place were lands belonging to the chief man of the island, named Publius, who received us and courteously entertained us for three days. (Acts 28:7)

Next, Sergius Paulus. Some like to say that an inscription for this proconsul has been found. If you dig into it, you find that Soloi, on Cyprus’s north coast, did yield an inscription mentioning a proconsul Paulus, but how its date-line should be read is disputed (about AD 50–54) and it carries only the name Paulus. Another fragment has been restored as naming a proconsul Quintus Sergius, and that restoration is disputed too. The name Paulus is not rare, either. So what we can say is that Luke’s title is correct, but that the inscription is about this same man can only be called possible. I have included this example precisely so that you can see that sometimes checking turns up only a possibility, and when it does, we say it just that way.

The scholar Craig Keener later wrote a four-volume commentary on Acts, reading the book within the tradition of ancient historical writing. Hemer also noticed that the sailing details and the ship’s vocabulary in chapter 27 carry the marks of someone who had dealt with sailors, and that several nautical terms even have a Latin flavor. That is solid homework. But the caution of Pervo’s school still stands, and below we will be honest about it.
A shipwreck that can be checked

The most striking case is the shipwreck in Acts 27. In 1848 a Scotsman named James Smith, a yachtsman who also studied ancient seafaring, simply took Luke’s chapter and studied it as a ship’s log. The later scholar Hemer likewise noticed that Luke uses a layman’s words and records the crew’s fear of running onto the Syrtis shoals and their sounding of the depth off Malta. Someone sitting at a desk making up a story could not write that seasick feeling.

Verse 29 is one I especially love: fearing that they would run aground on rocks, they cast four anchors from the stern and wished for daylight. That line has no theology in it at all, yet it captures what everyone on that ship felt in the dark.
Spiritual meaning: taking it seriously is itself a form of respect

Luke was willing to put in so much work because he believed these matters deserved to be taken seriously. Brothers and sisters, how do you treat the word of God? If a physician could investigate this carefully to write a book, can we not also open the map one more time when we read the Bible, and ask one more question?
2. To be honest, there are still a few problems unsolved

All right, now please put away the hand that wanted to slap the table. In Acts 5, Gamaliel speaks in the council and mentions Theudas, who rose up in revolt with some four hundred followers. The time is around the AD 30s. But the Theudas in Josephus appears under the Roman procurator Fadus, around AD 44 to 46, which is about ten years after Gamaliel’s speech. Even more troublesome, Gamaliel also says that Judas the Galilean came after Theudas, and Judas belongs to AD 6.

Some say there was another Theudas of the same name, a name that was not rare. Some say Luke made a mistake. Others argue he misread Josephus. I want to tell you honestly that on this question there is no settled answer.
Do Luke and Paul match up?

In the twentieth century the German scholar Vielhauer argued that the Paul of Acts and the Paul of the letters conflict over the law and over natural theology. Recent studies mostly find the two closer than he said, but differences remain. Read Galatians and you see Paul opposing Peter to his face, with a lot of heat. In Acts everyone is much more polite. This difference can be explained by Luke’s selection of material, but let’s not pretend we cannot see it.

Then there is the date. Most scholars place it at AD 80 to 90, and some argue for earlier, while Pervo argues for the early second century. Witetschek, for his part, thinks the local color of Ephesus in the book, such as the Asiarchs, may reflect Luke’s own era more. Even whether the author was the physician Luke, critical scholarship has no agreed view.
Spiritual meaning: we do not need to cover for God

Some worry that talking about all this might shake faith. I think the other way around. Picture a family where a child alters the report card whenever the grades are bad. That family is actually tense. In a family that is truly secure, the report card can be laid out on the dinner table and looked at together.

One more thing needs clearing up. We often hear this story: the great archaeologist Ramsay did not believe, set out to overturn Luke, and came to faith as soon as he looked into it. The real Ramsay was indeed influenced by the Tübingen school, and after his fieldwork he did turn to hold Luke in high regard, writing St. Paul the Traveller and the Roman Citizen in 1895. But his later popular apologetic works were also criticized by scholars. A good story should be told more accurately than the rumor tells it.
3. Inscriptions can only walk you to the door
A stone from a city gate cannot believe for you

Brothers and sisters, Luke got the city officials right. Does that prove Jesus rose from the dead? No. However accurately Jin Yong, the novelist, writes the city of Xiangyang, that does not mean his hero Guo Jing ever really defended it. The caution of scholars like Pervo is reasonable: accurate local color does not guarantee that every event happened.
What it can do is this: it takes away your reason for setting this book aside as a legend in a fog. It makes you willing to turn to the page the author cares about most. What is written on that page?
This Jesus God raised up, to which we all are witnesses. (Acts 2:32)
The whole book staked on one thing

When Peter said this, he was in Jerusalem, within walking distance of the tomb. The place where they spoke was a place where they could be refuted on the spot. Paul, standing before King Agrippa, also dared to say that these things were not done in a corner.

What did these people put on the line? Acts records it all along the way: prison, flogging, stoning. Paul himself admitted it was all-in. If Christ has not been raised, your faith is vain. He left himself no way out. A faith that puts every stake on one public event actually makes me bold to examine it seriously.
If Christ has not been raised, your faith is vain; you are still in your sins. (1 Corinthians 15:17)
Spiritual meaning: let my witness have an address too

Brothers and sisters, today’s application is very practical. What Luke records is a faith with an address. What about yours? Can you name the time, the place and the people for something God has done in your life?

The Bible is my standard, so I examine it. Jesus is my example, so I walk into real streets and alleys too. And others cannot read my inscriptions. What they read is how I treat my family and how I treat my coworkers. Life first, then relationships, then ministry. The person you spend every day with is checking the historical details of the book that is you. Change your mindset, change your life, change how you live. This road has to reach the office and the dinner table.

The conclusion today is simple. Luke did his homework very well, and some questions are still unsolved. You do not need to shout victory because of a stone from a city gate, and you do not need to throw the book away because of Theudas. Read it as a book worth taking seriously.

If you have not yet believed, I invite you to take one weekend and read Acts as history, with a map and with your questions. Then ask yourself the hardest question of all: why were these people willing to lay down their very lives for this?

Lord of history, thank You that You do not work in a fog. You have entered our cities and our shipwrecks. Thank You that Your Son truly died and truly rose again. Reign in our streets and alleys, help us live out a witness that can be checked, and let Jesus receive all the glory. In Jesus’ name, amen.
1. Why does a “closed on Mondays” kind of detail make people believe? How far do you think it can support a story, and where does it stop?
2. When you hear about unsolved questions like Theudas, what is your first reaction: unease, curiosity, or relief? Why?
3. Can you name the time, the place and the people for something God has done in your life? Please share for two minutes.
Does the Bible Contradict Itself? Four Signs, One King
Give diligence to present yourself approved by God, a workman who doesn’t need to be ashamed, properly handling the Word of Truth. (2 Timothy 2:15)

Brothers and sisters, peace to you! Today we’re taking up a question people don’t quite dare to ask inside the church, even though they get asked it all the time outside the church: does the Bible contradict itself?

I suspect some of you have already been in this scene. A college classmate hands you his phone and says, “Look, someone online has put together a hundred contradictions in the Bible.” Your scalp goes numb, and all you want is to make a quick trip to the bathroom.

Today we aren’t going to hide. Let me start by showing you a real “difference.” When Jesus was crucified, there was a sign above His head. Mark says it read “THE KING OF THE JEWS.” Luke says “THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS.” Matthew says “THIS IS JESUS, THE KING OF THE JEWS.” John says “JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS.”

One sign, four versions! If the church had wanted to fake something, this would have been the easiest place to get to work: just turn the four sentences into one. But the church didn’t. In the second century AD a man named Tatian actually did edit the four Gospels into one book, and it circulated for about three hundred years in parts of the Syriac-speaking church. In the end, the church still chose the four separate books and handed the differences on to us untouched.
A group trying to cover up a problem doesn’t behave like that. So today I invite you to bring that same candor with you and walk three stretches of road with me.
1. First get your tools in hand: a difference is not a contradiction

A contradiction has a very strict definition: two statements that cannot both be true at the same time. Suppose I say, “I had a lunch box today,” and my wife says, “He had a pork chop today.” That is no contradiction. In Taiwan the lunch box we call a bento often comes with a pork chop on the rice, and that’s the one I ate. Only if she says, “He fasted today,” do we have something to talk about at home.
So when you see two passages that differ, don’t rush to panic, and don’t rush to argue either. The first step is to ask: do these two statements really exclude each other?
The first key is genre. Poetry exaggerates, Proverbs speaks in general rules, and parables are stories. You wouldn’t take a love poem from a wedding down to the household registration office.

The second key is selective narration. John says it very plainly: “Jesus did many other signs in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book.” The authors were selecting all along. One Gospel mentions one angel and another mentions two, and mentioning one doesn’t say there was only one.

The third key is translation. Acts chapter 9 says the men traveling with Paul were “hearing the sound.” In chapter 22, the Chinese Union Version, the classic Chinese Bible, says they did not hear it clearly, and our English says “they didn’t understand the voice.” That one Greek verb can mean hearing, and it can also mean understanding. You stand on a train platform, you can hear the announcement, and you still can’t make out the name of the station. It’s probably something like that.

The fourth key is manuscripts. 2 Kings says Ahaziah was twenty-two when he came to the throne, and 2 Chronicles says forty-two. Some manuscripts of the Septuagint and the Syriac version also have twenty-two in 2 Chronicles. Numbers are easy to get wrong in ancient copying, as anyone who has ever copied by hand will understand. Some scholars have proposed other ways of counting, and we’ll just honestly lay those out too.

The fifth key is ancient writing habits. The American scholar Michael Licona compared ancient biographies and found that authors often compressed time, rearranged the order and focused the camera on one person. That doesn’t mean they wrote carelessly. They were following the rules of their day. But some evangelicals also worry this key is being used too freely, and that debate is still going on.
Spiritual meaning: examining is itself an act of faith

Some people assume faith means not asking. But the Bible commends the Bereans for “examining the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so.” Brothers and sisters, the God who inspired Scripture isn’t afraid of being checked. Properly handling the word of truth is work we are told to give diligence to.
Now these were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, examining the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so. (Acts 17:11)
2. Field practice: the ones we can untangle and the ones still hanging
The death of Judas and the morning of the resurrection

Matthew says Judas “went away and hanged himself.” Acts says “falling headlong, his body burst open and all his intestines gushed out.” The common harmonization is that he hanged himself first and the body fell later. That makes sense. But the scholar Bart Ehrman argues that the two places even tell differently who bought the field and why it was called the field of blood, so they shouldn’t be forced together. I’m telling you both sides, and you can go and read them yourself.

Now look at the morning of the resurrection. How many women? One angel or two? Mark says it was when the sun had risen, and John says it was still dark. These variations are all there. But set the four side by side and you’ll see four points of agreement: the first day of the week, the women arrive first, the stone has been moved, and the tomb is empty.

If you asked the four kids in our family what happened last Lunar New Year, you would certainly get four versions, and even who knocked over the hot pot would be in dispute. But not one of those kids would tell you we didn’t go back to Grandma’s house that year.
The two genealogies: a headache even for the early church

From David to Joseph, the genealogies in Matthew and Luke are almost two separate lists. In the third century AD, Africanus proposed an explanation based on a man marrying his brother’s widow, and he was very honest about it: he admitted he could find no corroboration, only that he had no better answer. Another view says Luke records Mary’s family line, but her name does not appear in Luke’s list.

So to this day, this question has no agreed answer. In AD 405 Augustine wrote to Jerome that when he read a passage that seemed wrong, he would suspect a faulty manuscript, a translator who had missed the sense, or his own failure to understand. You see, these difficulties weren’t discovered in the internet age. Sixteen hundred years ago a pastor was already sitting at his desk scratching his head.

For many friends, the very first place they get stuck is in the first two chapters of the Bible. In chapter 1 the animals come before humans. In chapter 2, verse 19, the Chinese Union Version reads as if the beasts were made after the man. Critical scholars mostly conclude these are two sources.

We need to see two things here. One is translation: some English versions render this verse as God “had formed” them and some don’t, and translators really have made different judgments. The other is literary: the scholar Richard Hess points out that the genealogies in Genesis 4 to 5 and 10 to 11 set two passages side by side in just this way, telling the big picture first and then focusing on one place. It’s like a news report that gives you the aerial view first and then moves the camera into one house. Whether or not there were sources behind it, the order we have today was arranged by someone on purpose.
Spiritual meaning: real open cases have to be told honestly

Mark 2:26 says David ate the show bread “at the time of Abiathar the high priest,” while the Old Testament names the priest as Ahimelech. When Ehrman was young he wrote a paper on this verse at Princeton Theological Seminary, defending it with all his strength, and his professor wrote a comment whose gist was that perhaps Mark had simply made a mistake. He says that comment went straight through his heart.

In fairness I have to say that by his own account, the decisive reason he finally left the faith was the problem of suffering. But the story reminds us of something: if faith is built on “I can solve every single question,” one crack can bring the whole thing down. Evangelicals have several solutions to this verse. Some are quite reasonable, but not everyone is satisfied. We’re allowed to say, “I’m still looking into this one.”
The secret things belong to Yahweh our God; but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children forever, that we may do all the words of this law. (Deuteronomy 29:29)
3. Where does the foundation of faith sit?

We need to state our position clearly. The 1978 Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy holds that the original manuscripts of the Bible are true in all they say, including statements of history and science. It also says that round numbers, hyperbole and accounts that don’t meet modern standards of precision do not count as errors. The Lausanne Covenant of 1974 likewise affirms the inspiration, truthfulness and authority of Scripture.

There are also brothers and sisters who hold a view of limited inerrancy or infallibility: the Bible is completely reliable on faith and life, while details of history and nature may carry human limitations. Others talk about flexible inerrancy. These are family discussions around the dinner table. We can go as deep into them as we like, but there’s no need to throw one another out of the house over them.
God dares to use four witnesses

Have you ever wondered why God didn’t simply hand us one official record with a single unified line? I wouldn’t dare say I know all of God’s reasons, and this is only my own guess: a unified line is how a public relations department works, while witnesses have eyes of their own. According to church tradition, the four Gospels came from a tax collector, a co-worker of Peter, a doctor and a fisherman, each speaking of the same Jesus in his own voice. Luke tells Theophilus right at the start that he wrote after “having traced the course of all things accurately from the first.” That’s a man willing to account for his sources.

So what is at the center of this witness? Paul says it most briefly: “Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures.” If someone told me I could keep only one passage from the whole Bible, I would keep this one. All the other hard questions are worth looking into, but they all come after this.
Spiritual meaning: first get to know the One

Brothers and sisters, please notice the order. You don’t have to solve a hundred hard questions before you can come to Jesus. Look at Thomas. He said that unless he touched with his own hand, he would not believe. And how did the risen Lord respond?

Then he said to Thomas, “Reach here your finger, and see my hands. Reach here your hand, and put it into my side. Don’t be unbelieving, but believing.” Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:27-28)

The Lord didn’t scold him, and He didn’t hand him a study guide either. The Lord held out His nail-scarred hands. Those hands are the center of the answer: Christ died for our sins and rose again on the third day. The hard questions can be looked into slowly. This One you can get to know today.

Let me leave you with three sentences. First, the Bible is my standard, so all the more we must handle it properly and never defend it by pulling words out of context. Second, humility overcomes pride: one “I don’t know the answer to this one yet” is a better witness than an hour of forcing an argument. Third, people matter more than tasks. When a friend comes to you with those hundred contradictions, that person matters far more than that debate. First ask him, “Why does this question matter to you?” Very often there’s a whole story hiding behind the question.

This week’s action: choose one of today’s examples, open the two passages yourself and compare them. Write one sentence that starts “What I see is,” then one that starts “What I still don’t understand is,” and bring them to your small group.

Let us pray together: Faithful Lord, thank you that you are not afraid of my questions. Give me an honest heart that can examine and can also admit what I don’t yet understand. Above all, through the Bible, let me know Jesus, the One who died and rose again for me. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
1. Is there a question about the Bible you’ve never dared to ask? If you’re willing, tell the group about it, and share why you didn’t dare to ask it back then.
2. Of the five keys, which one gave you the most new insight? Try to explain it using one of the examples from today.
3. If a friend asked you, “Doesn’t the Bible contradict itself?” how would you respond to him as a person, and not only to his question?
War and Cruelty in the Old Testament: No Makeup on God, and No Torn Pages
He who has seen me has seen the Father. (John 14:9)

Brothers and sisters, friends, peace to you! I hesitated for a long time before giving today’s lesson. Every preacher has certain passages he doesn’t quite dare read on a Sunday morning. Today we are going to read them anyway.

Look at Deuteronomy 20:16: “you shall save alive nothing that breathes.” Now look at 1 Samuel 15:3: “kill both man and woman, infant and nursing baby, ox and sheep, camel and donkey.” Nursing baby. Friends, anyone who has ever held an infant feels something twist inside when they read those two words. If you felt that twist, congratulations. Your conscience is working perfectly well.

Let me be clear first about three things I will not do today. First, I won’t tell you this is actually simple. Second, I won’t ask you to swallow your doubts. Third, I won’t announce at the end that the problem has been solved. Dr. Christopher Wright is a highly respected evangelical Old Testament scholar who wrote a whole book about the God he doesn’t understand, and when he comes to this subject he admits that he hasn’t found a good enough answer. Since he says that, if I stand up here and make it all sound too smooth, you should be on your guard. Today’s goal is a small one: so that the next time you read these passages, you don’t have to close the book, and you don’t have to shut down your conscience. You may still have questions when we’re done, and that’s fine. Going on to know Jesus with your questions in hand is far better than having no questions and not knowing Him.
1. First, let’s put everything on the table

There are three common ways people read these passages. The first is called “skip it.” Your Bible reading plan reaches Joshua and the pages turn especially fast, like driving past an accident with your eyes fixed straight ahead. The second is called “force it down.” Everything God does is right, so no questions allowed. That sounds full of faith, and yet even Abraham dared to ask God, “Shouldn’t the Judge of all the earth do right?” The third is called “tear it out.” The God of the Old Testament is too frightening, so I’ll just take the New. Marcion walked that road in the second century, and the church did not follow him.

There’s one more we need to be especially careful about, and I call it “too good at explaining.” A few quick sentences clear God of all charges, and then everyone is invited to turn to the next chapter. A friend who hears that won’t come to faith. He’ll simply conclude that Christians have rather flexible consciences.
What our friends across the table are asking

Let’s listen first to the voices from the other side. In The God Delusion Dawkins made a great deal out of the God of the Old Testament. Many of you may have heard about that. Two other people are even more worth hearing. The philosopher Wesley Morriston argues seriously that these commands are themselves strong evidence that the Bible contains errors, and that rather than say God ordered the destruction of a people, we should say the text got it wrong. Then there is Robert Warrior, an Osage Native scholar, whose words are hard to forget. Everyone loves the Exodus story, he says, the slaves going free. But he reads it through Canaanite eyes, and in the second half of the story he identifies with the people being driven out.

Friends, this isn’t just arguing for the sake of it. In history there really were people who held a Bible in one hand and a gun in the other and treated Native peoples as Canaanites. In Taiwan, in Malaysia, in New Zealand, the history of Indigenous peoples and colonization is no stranger to us. So this question has to be answered on our knees. Let’s not rush to be first with an answer from our mouths.
Shouldn’t the Judge of all the earth do right? (Genesis 18:25)
Spiritual meaning: you can come to God with your questions

When Abraham asked that, God did not rebuke him. When the people in the Psalms asked “how long,” those words were collected into the Bible. The prophet Habakkuk fired off question after question, and that book is named after him. So asking God honestly is itself part of faith.
2. Three serious answers, and the wound in each
The first: this is the language of battle reports

Friends in the school of Copan and Flannagan say you need to get to know ancient battle reports first. Around 1208 BC the Egyptian Pharaoh Merneptah set up a stele that reads, “Israel is laid waste, his seed is not.” And what happened? Israel was doing just fine. Today a sports headline says “Bloodbath for the Visitors,” and nobody calls the police, because everyone understands that language.

They also point to clues inside the Bible. Joshua says no Anakim were left, and then Caleb goes off to drive out the Anakim. Judges opens with a long list of Canaanites who were not driven out. Deuteronomy 7 says to destroy them, and also says not to intermarry with them. If everyone is dead, who is left to marry? And Exodus says they will be driven out “little by little.” So they conclude that the weight of the command is on expulsion, and that “genocide” is not an accurate word.

This explanation is powerful, and I have personally benefited from it. Where is the wound? In 1 Samuel 15, Saul is rebuked precisely because he left someone alive. How does that count as hyperbole? Even William Lane Craig, who also defends God here, thinks the hyperbole theory has a hard time fully fitting this passage. And even if not one child actually died, the question “How could God give such an order?” is still standing there.
The second: this is the verdict of the Judge

The second answer accepts it literally. Genesis 15 says, “the iniquity of the Amorite is not yet full.” God waited more than four hundred years. Leviticus 18 mentions passing children through the fire to Molech. This school says that life is God’s gift and God has the right to take it back, and that this was a one-time judgment, specific in time and place, which cannot be repeated. God treated Israel the same way, which is why Judah later went into exile.

Where is the wound? What sin has a nursing child committed? Some say that the children were received by God after death. Critics answer right away: then how do you explain that to the soldier holding the sword? Will he ever sleep at night again for the rest of his life? Besides, nearly every description of the Canaanites we have today comes from their opponents. They themselves left us very few words.
The third: look back from Jesus

The third answer comes from brothers such as Eric Seibert and C. S. Cowles. Jesus teaches us to love our enemies, they say, and the Father He revealed is the true God. The Old Testament depictions must be distinguished from Him, because they show God as ancient people understood Him under the influence of their culture. I deeply respect their hearts, because they too are concerned for God’s name. The wound is this: Jesus Himself accepted the Old Testament, and He also spoke of judgment. Most evangelicals will ask, once we are allowed to say of certain verses “this isn’t God,” who gets to draw that line? Wright takes a different road. He thinks both the history and the command have to be taken seriously, while honestly admitting that it still distresses him. Trimm’s 2022 book surveys all the various proposals and does not claim to have solved it either.

By the way, the archaeology isn’t simple either. Scholars such as Ronald Hendel think that Jericho and Ai were uninhabited in that period and that Israel emerged gradually; conservative scholars read it differently. But notice this, everyone: even if the fighting in history wasn’t so terrible, the question of why the text writes about God this way has not gone away.
Spiritual meaning: letting God be God and people be people

I’ve described all three roads and shown you the wounds in each, because I don’t want to pick one for you and then pretend it has no wound. Human limitation is not an excuse for laziness. It’s our real situation. We can say two sentences at the same time: I don’t understand this yet, and I still trust. If someone assures you that his explanation has no holes in it, please ask him a few more questions.
“For my thoughts are not your thoughts, and your ways are not my ways,” says Yahweh. (Isaiah 55:8)
3. All of this must finally come to the cross
The line was not drawn by bloodline

There are two people I’d ask you to remember. One is Rahab, a Canaanite and a prostitute, who said, “Yahweh your God, he is God in heaven above, and on earth beneath.” Her whole household was saved, and her name entered the genealogy of Jesus. The other is Achan, an Israelite through and through, who disobeyed and took what was devoted to destruction, and his end was terrible. I don’t find that passage easy reading either. But look: this book does not portray God as a war god who protects only one nation. God Himself warned Israel, “Not for your righteousness or for the uprightness of your heart do you go in to possess their land.”

The slavery laws are like this too. Some provisions were ahead of their time: knock out a slave’s tooth and you must set him free, and a slave who has escaped to you must not be handed back. Other provisions sting when we read them today. If a slave who has been beaten lasts a day or two (our Chinese Union Version reads it as dying a day or two later), “he shall not be punished, for the servant is his property.” Copan thinks that God, working in a situation of hardened human hearts, was leading people upward one step at a time. When Jesus spoke about divorce He also said, “Moses, because of the hardness of your hearts, allowed you to divorce your wives.” Critics ask: why not just abolish it outright? I don’t have an elegant answer to that question either.

Here I’m going to speak very firmly. Whichever explanation you hold, today no person, no church and no nation has the right to use these passages to kill, to seize land, to oppress any people, or to hit anyone at home. If someone says God told him to do this, stay away from him, and call the police if necessary. If you have been hurt by war, by violence, or by someone acting in God’s name, that is not your fault, and it is not God’s heart. Please find a pastor you can trust and qualified professionals, and get yourself safe first.
Spiritual meaning: He did not swing the sword; He went up to the cross

Philip said to Jesus: show us the Father. Jesus answered, “He who has seen me has seen the Father.” So what do we see? When the disciples wanted to call fire down from heaven, He turned and rebuked them. When Peter drew his sword, He said, “Put the sword into its sheath.” And then the most innocent One in the world, instead of making anyone else’s blood flow, was nailed up there Himself.
He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we, having died to sins, might live to righteousness. (1 Peter 2:24)

Friends, the cross hasn’t untied every verse of Deuteronomy for me. But it has answered the question I fear most: is God a God who doesn’t care when people bleed? At Calvary He bled in person. A Judge who is willing to do that is One I can entrust with what I still don’t understand.

The Bible is my standard, so I will read the hard passages too, and I will read all the way through to Christ. Jesus is my example, so my attitude toward my enemies must follow His on the cross and not my temper. Humility overcomes pride, so when a friend comes and asks, I can say plainly, “I don’t have an answer to this yet.” Sometimes that one sentence is a better witness for the Lord than ten pages of notes. This week please read Joshua 2 and 6, pay attention to Rahab, and then write down one real question you have for God and bring it to your small group.

Lord, Judge of all the earth, these passages distress us, and we do not want to pretend otherwise. Forgive our carelessness when we do not understand, and forgive the cruelty that people in history have done in Your name. For all who have been hurt in this way, please comfort and protect them Yourself. Fix our eyes on the One on the cross, and teach us to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with You. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
1. Which of these passages distresses you the most? In the past, have you usually dealt with them by skipping, forcing them down, tearing them out, or being too good at explaining?
2. Of the three answers, which do you find most persuasive? What do you make of its wound?
3. If a friend who doesn’t believe asked you this question, how would you begin? Practice in pairs, with one minute only, and include the sentence “I don’t understand this yet.”
The Bible and Science: Don’t Force It to Answer Questions It Isn’t Answering
All things were made through him. Without him, nothing was made that has been made. (John 1:3)

Brothers and sisters, friends, peace to you! May I ask: what time did the sun come up this morning? The weather presenter will tell you, 6:12. Has an astronomer ever phoned in to correct her, saying, Miss, the sun did not rise, the earth rotated? No. Because everyone knows what she means. Ecclesiastes says it too: “The sun also rises, and the sun goes down.” If you use that verse to prove the Bible does not understand astronomy, then you would have to sue the weather bureau as well.

But this question has genuinely hurt quite a few people. Some young people hear one view in Sunday school and another when they get to university, and caught in the middle, they do not dare to ask, and in the end they quietly leave the church. And some seekers say, the moment they open their mouths, I studied science and engineering; that book is too ancient. Today’s message is meant to help us lay this question out in the open. We are not here to defeat science, and we are not here to find scientists to endorse the Bible. We only want to ask one thing clearly: what question is this book really trying to answer?
1. Two books, and a God who is willing to stoop down

In 1605 the Englishman Francis Bacon wrote The Advancement of Learning, and in it he spoke of two books: the book of God’s word and the book of God’s works. He urged people to study both diligently, only not to mix them together. You read the Bible to know God; when you look at the starry sky or slice a cell, you are also reading His handiwork. The Author is the same, the genre is different. It is like a letter home from the same mother and a prescription she gets from the herbal doctor: you would not read the prescription to find out how she feels, and you would not take the letter to the pharmacy.

Going back more than a thousand years earlier, Augustine wrote a passage that today’s preachers should post on their desks. He said that when a Christian talks nonsense about astronomy and geography and says this is what the Bible means, so that those who know better laugh to hear it, it is shameful and dangerous. Why dangerous? Because people will think: you got all this wrong, so how can I believe what you say about the resurrection? A warning from sixteen hundred years ago is still fresh today.

Now let me bring in Calvin. Many people think of him as someone so stern he never smiled, but what he says about the “two great lights” in Genesis 1:16 is very interesting. He says that astronomers know Saturn is larger than the moon; it is just far from us. Moses did not say anything wrong. He was writing for all ordinary people, so he used the way of speaking that everyone sees when they look up.

Calvin also used a lovely picture: God speaks to us the way a nurse speaks baby talk to a little child. This is what we call “accommodation.” When you say to a two-year-old, “Come, eat yummy-yummy,” nobody says your Chinese has gotten worse, and nobody says you are deceiving him. You simply love him, so you get down to his level.
The heavens declare the glory of God. The expanse shows his handiwork. (Psalm 19:1)
Spiritual meaning: the God who stoops down

Think about it, brothers and sisters. The Creator of the universe was willing to speak with ancient shepherds in words they could understand, and that in itself is grace. He did not wait until humanity invented the telescope before He spoke. He talked about stars with Abraham, about sheep with David, and about fishing nets with fishermen. He has always been crouching down to speak with us.
2. Pits that history has stepped into
The Galileo story, told wrongly by both sides

Let’s talk about Galileo. The church often does not want to tell the story, and our anti-religious friends tell it with a bit too much enthusiasm. What actually happened was this: in 1616 the advisers of the Roman Curia judged the view that the sun is at the center of the universe to be a heretical proposition. In 1633 Galileo was tried, found “vehemently suspect of heresy,” forced to recant publicly, and spent the rest of his life under house arrest. That is true, and it is something the church ought to grieve over. In 1992 Pope John Paul II publicly acknowledged that the theologians of that time had made a mistake.

But what about the dungeon and the torture that everyone has heard about? The historian Finocchiaro checked the sources. Galileo was threatened with the instruments of torture but was not put to the question. He also hardly spent any time in prison, and in Rome he even had servants to wait on him. Among the contributors to the book Galileo Goes to Jail and Other Myths are scholars who are not believers. You see, telling the story accurately is good for everyone.

Protestants should not be too pleased with themselves, either. In 1539 Luther chatted about Copernicus at the dinner table, and a student wrote down what he said: he believed the Bible, because it was the sun that Joshua commanded to stand still, not the earth. As for the Calvin quotation circulating on the internet, “Who will dare to place the authority of Copernicus above that of the Holy Spirit?”, the historian Rosen looked into it and found no evidence for it. It was reconstructed from memory by people later on. Calvin did preach a sermon criticizing the claim that “the sun does not move,” but he did not name Copernicus, and scholars still cannot say for sure what he thought. Brothers and sisters, even the sharp words attributed to someone need to be checked.

The most interesting figure of that time was Cardinal Bellarmine. In a letter of 1615 he wrote that if someone really did prove that the earth goes around the sun, then we should say we had not understood those passages, and not that Scripture is wrong. He just did not believe such a proof existed. The first half of that sentence is for every generation of us. When our understanding of Scripture does not fit established facts, let’s not rush to declare who is wrong. Perhaps we have not yet understood the text.

And what about Joshua’s sun? Joshua 10 says, “The sun stood still, and the moon stayed.” Some brothers and sisters believe this was a real miracle, recorded from the point of view of a person standing on the ground. Others notice that the text itself says this is written in the book of Jashar, and the passage carries the rhythm of poetry. Galileo even came up with an explanation in which his sun-centered view fit this passage better than his opponents’ did, though even he treated it only as a debating move. Whichever way you read it, there is no need to invite Joshua to be a professor of astronomy.
The temptation of “the Bible said it long ago”

Today’s pit is the other way around. Someone says enthusiastically: Job said long ago that the earth hangs in space, how amazing! You open Job 26:7: God “hangs the earth on nothing.” It is indeed beautiful. But turn to chapter 38, and God asks Job again: “What were its foundations fastened on? Or who laid its cornerstone?” And 1 Samuel says: “The pillars of the earth are Yahweh’s.” If chapter 26 is science, then what are the pillars and the cornerstone?

Chinese readers have one more special pit. The Chinese Union Version of Isaiah 40:22 reads “God sits above the great circle of the globe.” Wow, the globe! But the original speaks of a circle or an arc, and the word for “globe” is the translators’ choice. English Bibles say simply “the circle of the earth,” and the very next phrase says He spreads out the heavens “like a tent to dwell in.” These are all poetry. To tie the Bible to this year’s science is to tie it to a ship that gets replaced every few decades. Whenever science makes a correction, your faith capsizes along with it.
It is he who sits above the circle of the earth, and its inhabitants are like grasshoppers; who stretches out the heavens like a curtain, and spreads them out like a tent to dwell in, (Isaiah 40:22)
Spiritual meaning: don’t collect Isaiah’s prize for him

What Isaiah wanted to say to the exiled people was: look at the God who sits on high. What are the nations before Him? Why are you discouraged? We do not need to win Isaiah an astronomy prize he never meant to compete for. He already holds something much greater.
3. How to read Genesis 1, and the Word who became flesh

First, picture a night three thousand years ago. No streetlights, no telescopes, and the sky comes down like an enormous canopy, one that can even drop water. The scholar Seely holds that the “expanse” in Genesis reflects exactly that solid dome in the ancient mind. Poythress, who also wrote in the Westminster Theological Journal, disagrees, saying the text only describes what people see and does not put forward a physical theory. Both take the Bible seriously, and they are still debating today. We need not rush to choose a side on this question, but it at least reminds us that to read Genesis, we should first sit down in the ancient reader’s seat.

How should Genesis 1 be read? Take a deep breath, everyone, because we are not going to fight. Brothers and sisters who hold a young earth read the six days literally. Those who hold an old earth think the “days” can be long periods. The literary framework view notices the carefully arranged structure, where the first three days form the realms and the last three fill them with inhabitants. And there is Professor Walton’s view, that this chapter is about God establishing the cosmos as His temple, giving it functions, and then taking up residence.

Each of the four views has people who love the Lord and hold to the authority of Scripture, each has its strengths, and each has its difficulties. The Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy stresses that the Bible’s reliability is not limited to the realm of faith, while also acknowledging that the Bible contains observational descriptions of natural phenomena. Today I am not going to rule for you. I ask only one thing: let’s not drive a brother or sister out of the door over this question, and let’s not block an unbelieving friend from coming in. God is the Creator; that is the core. On the rest, we search the Scriptures and love one another as we go.
Spiritual meaning: He became that Word
Let’s return to “accommodation.” When did God crouch down the lowest to speak? At Christmas.
The Word became flesh and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the only born Son of the Father, full of grace and truth. (John 1:14)

The Gospel of John begins by saying that all things were made through the Word, and a few lines later, this Word became flesh. The Lord who holds all things together became a baby who could not speak, and later went to the cross and rose on the third day. Science can measure the distances to the stars, which is its glory, and we thank God for it. But no telescope can tell you that the One who made the stars loves you and was willing to die for you. That sentence can only be read in another book.

The Bible is my standard, so I read it according to its genre: poetry as poetry, history as history. Humility overcomes pride, so I can say: this much I know on this question, and beyond that I do not know. People matter more than tasks, so a brother who sees things differently from you matters more than winning that debate. This is also a change of mindset: from being afraid of science to looking at every discovery with a heart of worship. If you have a child studying science or engineering, please pray for him, encourage him to be a good scientist, and let him know that the church is always a place where questions can be asked.

Lord who created heaven and earth, thank You for being willing to crouch down and speak to us, even becoming flesh and dying on the cross. Forgive us for sometimes using the Bible to cover our ignorance, and sometimes using knowledge to cover our pride. Give us minds that fear You, that dare to explore and dare to admit they do not know. Let us worship You through both of Your books. In Jesus’ name, amen.

2. How do the two pictures of the weather presenter and the nurse help you understand “accommodation”? Where are the limits of this idea? How do we keep it from being used to explain everything away?

The Book That Changes Lives: A Thread Across Sixteen Hundred Years
For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword (Hebrews 4:12)

Brothers and sisters, friends, peace to you! Please look at the Bible in your hands, or the Bible app on your phone. It weighs less than a kilogram, or perhaps nothing at all. Yet this book once made a professor of rhetoric in the Roman Empire collapse in tears under a tree, made a German monk feel that he had walked into paradise, and made an English pastor so earnest that it was almost too much suddenly find his heart warmed.

Today I am going to tell the stories of several people, and every one of them can be traced to its source. Before I begin, let me set a rule: I will not prettify the stories. There are already far too many over-polished testimonies in this world, and all of you can hear it. True stories have delays, failures, and places that were still not cleaned up even in old age. That is exactly why I dare to lay them before you.
1. A thread across sixteen hundred years

AD 386, Milan. Augustine was already a successful professor of rhetoric, with a name and eloquence, but his private life had him in chains, and he could not break free on his own. He writes in Book VIII of his Confessions that on that day he went into the garden and wept aloud under a fig tree. Just then he heard from next door the voice of a child, singing over and over: “Take up and read, take up and read.”

He remembered the story of the monk Antony, so he went back and opened Paul’s letters, and read Romans 13: “not in reveling and drunkenness, not in sexual promiscuity and lustful acts, and not in strife and jealousy. But put on the Lord Jesus Christ.” He said he did not need to read any further. His friend Alypius took the book and read on to the next sentence: “Now accept one who is weak in faith.” Alypius said: this sentence is about me. Lovely, isn’t it? One reads that he must put on Christ, another reads that he is to be accepted. The same book, and each receives his own.

To be honest, the Confessions was written about ten years later, and scholars have noticed that the scene has been arranged for literary effect. But modern scholars mostly do not deny the event itself because of that. That a piece of writing is well crafted does not make the thing false.
Luther with the open gate, and that evening in London

About eleven hundred years later, it was Luther’s turn to wrestle with Romans. Looking back in 1545, he said he had once hated the very words “God’s righteousness” in Romans 1:17, thinking it was the club God uses to beat people. Not until he understood the second half, “the righteous shall live by faith,” did he feel, he said, as if he had been born again and had gone through open gates into paradise. Scholars still debate in what year this happened, and some think he came to understand it gradually. But that gate truly opened.

Two hundred years after that, 24 May 1738: the English pastor John Wesley. This gentleman was so earnest that people laughed at how strictly he kept the rules, and when he went to America as a missionary he returned defeated. That morning at five o’clock he opened the New Testament and read in 2 Peter that God “has granted to us his precious and exceedingly great promises,” and before going out he came across another line: “You are not far from God’s Kingdom.” In the evening, rather unwillingly, he went to a meeting on Aldersgate Street, where someone was reading Luther’s preface to Romans. He wrote in his journal that at about a quarter before nine, his heart felt strangely warmed, and he felt that he did trust in Christ, Christ alone, for salvation.

Brothers and sisters, do you see the thread? Paul wrote Romans, Augustine read it, Luther read it, Luther wrote a preface, and Wesley heard it. This book is like a relay baton, passed from Rome to Milan, to Germany, to London, and now to your hands.

For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the dividing of soul and spirit, of both joints and marrow, and is able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart. (Hebrews 4:12)
Spiritual meaning: it can pierce you

The text says it can pierce and divide. A motivational book makes you comfortable when you finish it, but this Book sometimes makes people uncomfortable, because it is reading you. The first sentence Augustine read did not pat him on the head. It pointed straight to the place he could least let go of.
2. The cost of change, and what was never fully cleaned up

Everyone knows how to sing “Amazing Grace.” Its author, John Newton, had been a slave trader in his youth. In 1748 his ship ran into a violent storm in the North Atlantic, and on board he read the New Testament and took hold of Luke 11:13: “how much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him?” The story is usually told up to this point, and then the song comes in and the whole room is moved.

But please listen to the end. After he came to faith he kept working on slave ships and even became a captain, and only left the sea when he had a stroke in 1754, and afterward he went on investing in the trade. He had believed, and still his hands were gripping people. It was a long time later, in 1788, that he published a pamphlet publicly exposing the slave trade, calling himself an active instrument in that business and saying he would be ashamed of it all his life. By then it had been thirty-four years since he left. In 1807 Britain passed the act abolishing the slave trade, and he died at the end of that year.

Brothers and sisters, this story has more power than the simplified version. It tells us that human conscience has blind spots, and God’s word has to be peeled back layer by layer. Luther was the same: in his old age he wrote viciously anti-Jewish texts, which is a stain on him that cannot be avoided. After Aldersgate, Wesley wrote early the next year that he was not a Christian. So please do not use these people to press yourself down, thinking that others become perfect the moment they believe. And do not, when you see the failures of Christians, say that this book has no use.
A reluctant man, and a dinner table

C. S. Lewis, the author of the Chronicles of Narnia, said that in his room at Oxford he knelt and admitted that God was God, and that he was probably the most dejected and reluctant convert in all England that night. Accepting that Jesus is the Son of God came later still, and his friends Tolkien and Dyson stayed up talking with him until past midnight in between. He later wrote in a letter that the story of the Gospels is a myth that really happened. You see, he did not turn around from reading a single verse, either. God uses books, and He also uses friends.

Let me tell of two people closer to our own time. Rosaria Butterfield was a professor of English and women’s studies at Syracuse University, and at that time she was active in the lesbian community. In 1997 she wrote an article criticizing a Christian movement, and later received a letter from a pastor, Ken Smith. He did not argue with her. He simply asked gently: How did you arrive at these views? How do you know you are right? Do you believe in God? She threw the letter away, then picked it out of the trash, and left it on her desk for a week. Later she became friends with the pastor and his wife, ate many meals with them, and read the Bible in many translations, several times through. In 1999 she came to faith. She wrote that she counted the cost and did not like the number on the other side of the equals sign. We do not tell this story to attack anyone. What I ask you to notice is the dinner table, and the couple’s two years of patience.

Nabeel Qureshi’s parents were Ahmadiyya Muslims from Pakistan. He was devout from childhood and trained to defend Islam. In 2001 at university he saw his classmate David Wood reading the Bible on his own, thought it strange, and the two began to debate and also became friends. He examined the evidence, asked questions, and asked God for dreams, and he says he had several significant ones; in his most painful time, he opened the New Testament and felt the text answering him verse by verse. Coming to faith cost him most of his Muslim friends, and he said it was the most painful thing he had ever done. This was his own personal road, and our Muslim friends do not necessarily agree with his conclusion, which we should also respect. He died of stomach cancer in 2017, only thirty-four years old.
Spiritual meaning: this Book does not sell success

Please notice that reading the Bible did not buy Qureshi a long life, and it did not preserve Butterfield’s old world for her. The Bible has never marketed itself that way. What it gives is a Lord who walks with you, whom not even death can separate you from. So are there any statistics? There are. The Center for Bible Engagement in the United States reports that people who engage with the Bible four or more days a week report markedly less drunkenness and less viewing of pornography. This is a questionnaire, and the organization also promotes Bible reading, and people who are already serious naturally read more, so we cannot say that four days guarantees change. We can take it as an encouragement, but not as a formula.
3. The center of this Book is a Person
Some read it and did not change

To be fair, there are also people who read it all their lives and did not change. There were slaveholders in the American South who read the Bible, and the New Testament scholar Bart Ehrman knows it better than most of us, yet he says the problem of suffering finally led him away from the faith. Jesus also said to the people of His day who knew the Scriptures best:
“You search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life; and these are they which testify about me. Yet you will not come to me, that you may have life. (John 5:39-40)
So the key is this sentence: “come to me.” The book itself is not magic. It is a window. You can keep studying the wood of the window frame, or you can lean out and see the One standing outside.
Spiritual meaning: the stranger on the road

On the evening of Easter, two disciples were walking the road to Emmaus, utterly disappointed. A stranger walked with them and began with Moses and all the prophets. Only later did they recognize that it was Jesus, and they said to one another, “Weren’t our hearts burning within us?” Seventeen hundred years later, Wesley’s heart was warmed too. Why does it still warm after so long? Because the One who opened the Scriptures has risen, and He is alive. What Romans showed Luther was the righteousness this Lord accomplished for us on the cross. So when we read the Bible, we go to meet a living Lord.

The Bible is my standard, so start small. If you have never read it, open John today, a chapter a day, and finish in twenty-one days. You can use the 321 Interactive Bible, too. Before you read, pray a simple prayer: If You are real, please let me know You. The Holy Spirit is my guide, so when you finish, ask: what does He want me to change today? People matter more than tasks, so find someone to read with. Perhaps what someone needs is your dinner table, and your two years of patience.

Lord Jesus, Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light for my path. Thank You that You spoke to sinners like Augustine, Luther and Newton, and that You speak to me today. Holy Spirit, shine Your light on my blind spots, so that I do not only read but am willing to obey, and am changed by You all my life. Let our hearts burn again, and make us a baton in the hands of others. In Jesus’ name, amen.
